country.name: Australia
country.tagline: The country that kept phylloxera out of its oldest vineyards, then taught the world to drink Shiraz, Riesling under screwcap and hundred-year-old Tawny.

stats.note: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026): 159 kha of vineyard, 11.3 mhl of wine in 2025, fifth in the world and the largest producer in the Southern Hemisphere. Wine Australia's National Vintage Report 2026 put the 2026 crush at 1.27 million tonnes, the smallest since 2000.

country.overview:
Australian wine is a story told in two scripts at once. One is industrial and brilliant: irrigated vineyards along the Murray, Darling and Murrumbidgee rivers that turned out clean, sunny, cheap wine in such volume that a kangaroo on a label became a global brand. The other is ancient and stubborn: gnarled, own-rooted Shiraz, Grenache and Mourvèdre in the Barossa and McLaren Vale planted by Silesian farmers and English gentlemen in the 1840s and 1850s, vines older than almost anything left standing in Europe. Both scripts matter, and the second exists because the first colonists' descendants were fanatical about quarantine.

Phylloxera reached Victoria in 1877 and laid waste to Geelong, Bendigo and much of the colony's young industry. South Australia shut its borders to vine material and has kept them shut ever since, policed today by Vinehealth Australia. The result is a living museum: the Langmeil Freedom block of Shiraz (1843), Cirillo's Grenache at Light Pass (1848), Hewitson's Old Garden Mourvèdre (1853), Penfolds' Block 42 Cabernet at Kalimna (1888), plus Tahbilk's 1860 Shiraz in Victoria, a pocket the louse never found. The Barossa Old Vine Charter, drafted by Yalumba in 2007, now registers these vines as Old (35 years plus), Survivor (70), Centenarian (100) and Ancestor (125). Old-vine fruit tends to be lower yielding and more even in ripening, and these vineyards are the reason a Barossa Shiraz can taste of place rather than of sunshine alone.

For most of its first 150 years Australia was a fortified-wine country. Port-style blends, sherry-style flor wines and the extraordinary liqueur Muscats of Rutherglen dominated until the 1960s. The pivot came from inside the biggest company: Max Schubert of Penfolds came home from Bordeaux and Jerez in 1950 and made the first experimental Grange Hermitage in 1951, a Shiraz built to age for decades. Management ordered him to stop in 1957; he kept going in secret. Grange became the national first growth, and the table-wine revolution followed: Hunter Semillon and Shiraz, Coonawarra Cabernet off the terra rossa, Clare and Eden Valley Riesling, and from the late 1960s the doctors' vineyards of Margaret River and the Yarra Valley.

The modern map is set by the Geographical Indication system. Wine Australia registers 28 zones (plus state and super-zone GIs such as South Eastern Australia), 65 regions and 14 subregions. They are lines on a map and nothing more: no rules on grape varieties, yields or winemaking, just the guarantee, enforced through the Label Integrity Program, that at least 85 percent of the wine comes from the place, variety and vintage on the label. That freedom explains why Australian producers can make Fiano in McLaren Vale or Nebbiolo in the Adelaide Hills without asking anyone, and why the more meaningful sub-divisions (the Barossa Grounds, McLaren Vale's districts, Margaret River's Wilyabrup, Tasmania's Tamar and Coal River valleys) are informal.

Climate is the great organiser. Inland, three irrigated regions (Riverland, Murray Darling and Riverina) still crush more than half the national tonnage. Along the southern coast, cold Southern Ocean air, altitude and latitude produce a mosaic of cool sites: Tasmania, with under 800 growing degree days, now supplies much of the country's best sparkling wine and Pinot Noir, while the Mornington Peninsula, Macedon Ranges, Adelaide Hills and Great Southern make Chardonnay and Pinot as taut as anything in the New World. Australia also gave the world a closure: in August 2000, fourteen Clare Valley Riesling producers bottled together under screwcap to escape cork taint, and within a decade most Australian and New Zealand wine followed.

The 2020s have been hard. China imposed anti-dumping duties of 116.2 to 218.4 percent on Australian bottled wine from late 2020, wiping out a market worth more than a billion Australian dollars a year, and lifted them only in March 2024. Red wine demand is falling worldwide, and growers in the warm inland are pulling out vines. The 2026 crush of 1.27 million tonnes was the smallest since 2000, 25 percent below the ten-year average, with reds down 29 percent. The industry that emerges will be smaller, cooler-climate and more site-specific, which is good news for anyone who cares about where wine comes from.

history.title: First Fleet vines at Farm Cove
history.text: Governor Arthur Phillip's First Fleet carried vine cuttings collected at Rio de Janeiro and the Cape of Good Hope, and planted them at Farm Cove on Sydney Harbour. Humidity and disease killed most of them, an early lesson that Sydney's climate was the wrong one.

history.title: Macarthurs and Blaxland
history.text: John Macarthur's family planted vines at Camden Park, and Gregory Blaxland shipped wine to London, where it won a silver medal from the Royal Society of Arts in 1823: the first sign that Australian wine could travel.

history.title: James Busby's cuttings
history.text: James Busby, a Scottish-born teacher of viticulture, toured the vineyards of Spain and France in 1831 and returned to Sydney in 1832 with cuttings of several hundred varieties. Planted at the Sydney Botanic Gardens, Camden Park and in the Hunter Valley, they seeded much of early Australian viticulture, including some of its Shiraz. Busby left for New Zealand in 1833 as British Resident.

history.title: Silesian Lutherans reach the Barossa
history.text: Prussian Lutherans fleeing religious pressure, sponsored by George Fife Angas and led by Pastor August Kavel, settled around Adelaide from 1838 and in the Barossa (Bethany) from 1842. They brought village farming, smallgoods, choirs and a habit of planting vines that their great-great-grandchildren still tend.

history.title: The Freedom vineyard
history.text: Christian Auricht planted Shiraz at what is now Langmeil, Tanunda. Still producing as the Freedom 1843 Shiraz, it is generally cited as the oldest continuously producing Shiraz vineyard in the world.

history.title: Dr Penfold's Grange
history.text: Dr Christopher Rawson Penfold planted vines at his Magill cottage, The Grange, east of Adelaide, to make tonic wines for patients. His wife Mary ran the winery; the company became the biggest in the land.

history.title: Tahbilk's Shiraz
history.text: The Goulburn Vineyard Proprietary planted at Tahbilk on the Goulburn River. A small block of 1860 Shiraz survived phylloxera on its sandy soils and still makes the 1860 Vines Shiraz.

history.title: Phylloxera at Geelong
history.text: Phylloxera was confirmed near Geelong in 1877. Victoria ordered vineyards uprooted, then lost Bendigo and much of the north-east over following decades. South Australia banned imports of vines and later created a Phylloxera Board (now Vinehealth Australia), which is why its old vines survive on their own roots.

history.title: Penola Fruit Colony
history.text: John Riddoch subdivided land at Coonawarra into 10-acre blocks for settlers in 1890 and built a triple-gabled winery in 1891 to process their grapes. The strip of red soil over limestone became Australia's Cabernet heartland; the building is now Wynns Coonawarra Estate.

history.title: Grange Hermitage
history.text: Back from Bordeaux, Max Schubert made the first experimental Grange Hermitage at Magill. Told to stop in 1957, he made the 1957 to 1959 vintages in secret. Grange turned Australia from a fortified-wine nation into a table-wine one.

history.title: The doctors' vineyards
history.text: Agronomist John Gladstones published research in 1965 suggesting Margaret River resembled Bordeaux. Dr Tom Cullity planted Vasse Felix in 1967, followed by Moss Wood, Cullen and Cape Mentelle; in Victoria Bailey Carrodus (Yarra Yering, 1969) and Dr John Middleton (Mount Mary, 1971) revived the Yarra Valley.

history.title: Geographical Indications
history.text: Amendments to the Australian Wine and Brandy Corporation Act created a Geographical Indications Committee, and the first zones and regions were registered from 1994 to 1996, to implement the 1994 wine agreement with the European Union. The Label Integrity Program, started in 1990, audits every claim.

history.title: Clare Valley screwcap
history.text: On 11 August 2000 fourteen Clare Valley wineries, including Grosset, Mount Horrocks, Taylors and Leasingham, announced they would bottle Riesling under screwcap to escape cork taint. The rest of Australia followed within a decade.

history.title: Barossa Old Vine Charter
history.text: Yalumba drafted a register of old vines, adopted by the Barossa's grape and wine association: Old Vine (35 years), Survivor (70), Centenarian (100) and Ancestor (125).

history.title: China tariffs
history.text: China imposed anti-dumping duties of up to 218.4 percent on Australian bottled wine from late 2020, closing what had been the largest export market by value. The duties were removed at the end of March 2024, but the market came back smaller.

history.title: Smallest crush since 2000
history.text: Wine Australia reported a 2026 crush of 1.27 million tonnes, 19 percent below 2025 and 25 percent below the ten-year average, as inland growers left red grapes unpicked or pulled out vines in response to soft demand.

country.classification:
Australia's Geographical Indications (GIs) are registered by Wine Australia's Geographical Indications Committee and protected under the Wine Australia Act 2013. They nest in a hierarchy: the GI 'Australia', the multi-state super zone 'South Eastern Australia' (all of New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania and parts of Queensland and South Australia), state GIs, then 28 zones (the 'Adelaide' super zone sits across three of them), 65 regions and 14 subregions. A region must be a single tract of land producing at least 500 tonnes a year from five or more vineyards of at least 5 hectares each, and be measurably distinct; a subregion must be substantially more homogeneous still.

The lines say nothing about how wine is made. There are no permitted-variety lists, yield caps or ageing rules. What the law enforces, through the Label Integrity Program, is truth in labelling: if a GI, a variety or a vintage appears on the label, at least 85 percent of the wine must match it; blends must list varieties in descending order. Some boundaries were fought over in court for years (Coonawarra was registered only in 2003, after a long dispute over which red-soil vineyards were in), which shows how much money a name carries.

Other protected terms matter too. The fortified-style terms Cream, Crusted, Ruby, Solera, Tawny and Vintage are 'quality wine terms' with set definitions. After the 2008 wine agreement with the EU, Australia retired European names: 'Tokay' became Topaque, Australian sherry became Apera (from 2011), and 'port' became Tawny or simply fortified. Rutherglen's producers run their own four-step ladder for Muscat and Topaque (Rutherglen, Classic, Grand, Rare). Informal sub-zoning has also grown: the Barossa Grounds study, McLaren Vale's district maps and Langton's Classification of Australian Wine (a market ranking, not a law) are where the finer distinctions live.
country.climate_soils:
Most Australian vineyards sit between 32 and 38 degrees south, in a band where a Mediterranean pattern of winter rain and dry summers meets the huge thermal mass of an arid continent. Without moderation they would be hot; the art of Australian site selection is finding the moderators. The Southern Ocean cools Margaret River, the Great Southern, the Limestone Coast, the Fleurieu and the Mornington Peninsula; altitude cools the Adelaide Hills, Eden Valley, Orange, Tumbarumba, the Macedon Ranges and the Granite Belt; latitude makes Tasmania the coolest state, with growing degree days below 800.

Wine Australia's own climate figures show the range. Riverland and Murray Darling run around 2,350 to 2,550 growing degree days (October to April) with under 180 mm of growing-season rain, so they are entirely irrigated. Barossa Valley sits at about 1,970 degree days, Coonawarra 1,570, the Yarra Valley 1,440 and the Macedon Ranges 1,390. The Hunter is the anomaly: warm (about 2,200) but wet in summer, with more than 550 mm of rain in the growing season, which explains its early-picked, low-alcohol Semillon.

The soils are some of the oldest on earth. Weathered, low in nutrients and often sandy over clay, they keep vigour in check. Famous exceptions are the terra rossa over limestone at Coonawarra, Padthaway, Wrattonbully and Watervale; the Cambrian greenstone of Heathcote; the ironstone, quartz and slate of Eden Valley; the deep Blewitt Springs sands of McLaren Vale; the gravelly loams over granite of Margaret River; the volcanic basalts of Orange and parts of the Yarra; and Tasmania's dolerite and basalt. Water is the limit everywhere: rights to the Murray and its tributaries, more than any GI, decide where the bulk of Australian wine can be grown.

grapes.name: Shiraz
grapes.note: The national red and the most planted grape. Barossa and McLaren Vale make it dense and chocolatey, Heathcote and the Grampians peppery, the Hunter medium-bodied and earthy, Canberra and the Yarra Rhône-like and often co-fermented with Viognier. Some of the world's oldest Shiraz vines are in the Barossa (1843) and at Tahbilk (1860).

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: Classic in Coonawarra, Margaret River (Wilyabrup), the Yarra Valley and Clare; often blended with Shiraz in the uniquely Australian Cabernet-Shiraz style.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: Swung from the oaky 1980s style to lean, struck-match wines from Margaret River (Leeuwin, the Gingin clone), Yarra, Mornington, Adelaide Hills, Beechworth and Tasmania; also the base of Tasmanian sparkling.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.note: Bone-dry, lime-scented and long-lived from Clare (Polish Hill, Watervale) and Eden Valley, with newer cool sites in the Great Southern, Henty and Tasmania. The variety that drove the screwcap switch.

grapes.name: Semillon
grapes.note: The Hunter's signature: picked early at 10 to 11 percent alcohol, unoaked, and transformed by ten years in bottle into toast and honey. Also blended with Sauvignon Blanc in Margaret River and made botrytised in the Riverina (De Bortoli Noble One).

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.note: Once dismissed as fortified fodder, now prized from old bush vines in McLaren Vale (Blewitt Springs) and the Barossa, made lighter and more perfumed.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Tasmania, Mornington Peninsula, Yarra Valley, Macedon Ranges, Gippsland (Bass Phillip) and the Adelaide Hills.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre (Mataro)
grapes.note: Old Barossa plantings (Hewitson's 1853 Old Garden) and the GSM blend with Grenache and Shiraz.

grapes.name: Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge and Muscadelle
grapes.note: The grapes behind Rutherglen Muscat and Topaque, Australia's great fortified wines.

grapes.name: Mediterranean newcomers
grapes.note: Fiano, Vermentino, Nero d'Avola, Montepulciano, Tempranillo, Touriga Nacional and Prosecco (King Valley): a response to heat, drought and a migrant heritage, especially in McLaren Vale, the Riverland and the King Valley.

regions.name: South Australia
regions.tagline: Half of Australia's wine and nearly all of its oldest vines, protected by a border the phylloxera louse never crossed.
regions.summary:
South Australia crushes roughly half of the national harvest and owns most of its famous names: Barossa Valley, Eden Valley, Clare Valley, McLaren Vale, Adelaide Hills, Coonawarra and the Riverland. It is also Australia's wine capital in an institutional sense, home to Wine Australia, the Australian Wine Research Institute, the University of Adelaide's Waite campus and Roseworthy, where generations of winemakers trained.

What makes the state unique is its quarantine. South Australia never had phylloxera, and strict controls on moving vines, machinery and even grapes across its borders mean that ungrafted vines planted in the 1840s still crop. Those old vineyards, concentrated in the Barossa, McLaren Vale and Langhorne Creek, are the backbone of its fine-wine reputation.
regions.history: Colonised as a free settlement in 1836, South Australia attracted religious dissenters, including the Silesian Lutherans who farmed the Barossa from 1842, and English and Scottish gentlemen such as John Reynell (McLaren Vale, 1838), Dr Christopher Penfold (Magill, 1844), Samuel Smith (Yalumba, 1849) and Joseph Seppelt (1851). The state became the centre of the fortified-wine industry in the late nineteenth century and, after the Second World War, of the table-wine revival led by Penfolds, Hardys, Orlando and Lindemans. Its GI hierarchy groups regions into zones: Barossa, Mount Lofty Ranges, Fleurieu, Limestone Coast, Lower Murray, Far North and The Peninsulas, with the 'Adelaide' super zone wrapping the first three.
regions.terroir: Climates range from the hot, irrigated Riverland (about 2,350 growing degree days and 148 mm of growing-season rain) to the cool, maritime Limestone Coast and the elevated Adelaide Hills and Eden Valley. Gulf St Vincent moderates McLaren Vale and Adelaide; Lake Alexandrina's 'Lake Doctor' breeze cools Langhorne Creek. Soils run from terra rossa over limestone in the south-east to sand, ironstone, schist and ancient quartzite in the Mount Lofty Ranges.
regions.grapes: Shiraz above all, then Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Chardonnay, Riesling and Mourvèdre; Mediterranean varieties such as Fiano, Vermentino, Nero d'Avola and Montepulciano are spreading fastest in McLaren Vale and the Riverland.
regions.styles: Full-bodied Shiraz and Cabernet, old-vine Grenache and GSM blends, bone-dry Riesling, cool-climate Chardonnay and sparkling from the Adelaide Hills, and historic fortifieds (Seppeltsfield's Tawny, Barossa 'Apera').
regions.classification: Zones: Barossa, Mount Lofty Ranges, Fleurieu, Limestone Coast, Lower Murray, Far North, The Peninsulas (plus the Adelaide super zone). Subregions: High Eden, Lenswood, Piccadilly Valley. Informal: the Barossa Grounds and the Barossa Old Vine Charter, McLaren Vale's district maps, Clare's Polish Hill River and Watervale.

regions.name: Victoria
regions.tagline: The gold-rush colony that phylloxera humbled, now the most varied wine state in Australia, from Rutherglen Muscat to Macedon sparkling.
regions.summary:
Victoria has more wine regions than any other state (21) and the widest stylistic range: thick, ancient Rutherglen Muscat, peppery Heathcote and Grampians Shiraz, Yarra Valley Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, Mornington Peninsula Pinot, Macedon Ranges sparkling, King Valley Prosecco, Beechworth's Giaconda Chardonnay and the irrigated volume of the Murray Darling.

In the 1880s Victoria was briefly Australia's largest producer and its wines took medals in Paris and Bordeaux. Phylloxera, found near Geelong in 1877, and the economic depression of the 1890s ended that boom. The modern revival is a story of individuals: doctors, engineers and refugees from city careers who replanted the Yarra, Mornington, Geelong and Macedon from the 1960s onwards.
regions.history: Swiss settlers led by Paul and Hubert de Castella and Guillaume de Pury planted the Yarra Valley from the 1840s to 1860s; Henry and Joseph Best planted Great Western in the 1860s; Rutherglen boomed on gold-rush money from 1858; Tahbilk was founded in 1860. Phylloxera spread from Geelong through Bendigo to the north-east, and by the 1920s Victorian table wine had nearly vanished, leaving fortifieds in Rutherglen and Glenrowan. Revivals came with Brown Brothers (Milawa), Balgownie (Bendigo, 1969), Yarra Yering (1969), Mount Mary (1971) and Domaine Chandon's arrival in 1986.
regions.terroir: Bass Strait and Port Phillip Bay cool the southern regions; the Great Dividing Range lifts the Macedon Ranges, Strathbogie Ranges, Upper Goulburn and Alpine Valleys above 500 m. North of the Divide, heat builds toward Rutherglen and the Murray. Soils are diverse: Cambrian greenstone at Heathcote, granite at Beechworth and Strathbogie, volcanic red earths in parts of the Yarra and Mornington, sandy loams at Tahbilk that kept phylloxera at bay.
regions.grapes: Shiraz, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Gris; Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge and Muscadelle in Rutherglen; Marsanne at Tahbilk; Italian varieties in the King Valley.
regions.styles: Fortified Muscat and Topaque, cool-climate Pinot and Chardonnay, sparkling (including the historic sparkling Shiraz of Great Western), peppery Shiraz, Prosecco.
regions.classification: Zones: Port Phillip, Central Victoria, North East Victoria, North West Victoria, Western Victoria and Gippsland (Gippsland has no registered regions). Subregions: Great Western (Grampians) and Nagambie Lakes (Goulburn Valley). Rutherglen Muscat has its own four-tier classification.

regions.name: New South Wales
regions.tagline: Where Australian wine began, and where the Hunter still makes the country's most singular white.
regions.summary: New South Wales holds the first vineyards of the colony and the second-largest crush, thanks to the irrigated Riverina around Griffith. Its fine-wine centre is the Hunter Valley, three hours north of Sydney, whose Semillon and medium-bodied Shiraz are unlike anything else in Australia. Up on the tablelands and western slopes of the Great Dividing Range, Orange, Mudgee, Hilltops, Tumbarumba and the Canberra District offer cooler, higher sites.
regions.history: From Farm Cove (1788) and Camden Park (1820s) the industry moved to the Hunter, where James Busby's Kirkton estate, George Wyndham's Dalwood (1828), Henry Lindeman's Cavendish (1843) and the Tyrrells (1858) planted. Maurice O'Shea's work at Mount Pleasant from the 1920s to 1956 set the Hunter's style. The Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area, opened in 1912, created the Riverina, where Italian families and the McWilliam, De Bortoli and Casella companies built volume brands such as [yellow tail].
regions.terroir: The Hunter is subtropical, hot and humid, with summer rain and cloud cover that temper the heat. The Central Ranges and Southern New South Wales regions climb to 600 to 1,400 m on basalt and granite; Orange's GI only covers land above 600 m. The Riverina is flat, hot and irrigated from the Murrumbidgee.
regions.grapes: Semillon, Shiraz and Chardonnay in the Hunter; Shiraz, Cabernet, Chardonnay and Riesling in the ranges; Semillon (including botrytised), Shiraz, Chardonnay and Durif in the Riverina.
regions.styles: Early-picked, long-lived Hunter Semillon; earthy Hunter Shiraz; Canberra Shiraz-Viognier; cool-climate Chardonnay and sparkling base from Tumbarumba and Orange; botrytis Semillon from the Riverina.
regions.classification: Zones: Hunter Valley, Central Ranges, Southern New South Wales, Big Rivers, South Coast, Northern Rivers, Northern Slopes and Western Plains. Subregions: Pokolbin, Broke Fordwich and Upper Hunter Valley (all within the Hunter region).

regions.name: Western Australia
regions.tagline: Small in volume, huge in reputation: Margaret River Cabernet and Chardonnay, and the cool granite country of the Great Southern.
regions.summary: Western Australia makes only around 3 to 4 percent of Australia's wine but a far larger share of its fine wine. Margaret River, planted on the advice of a scientist in the late 1960s, is one of the world's great places for Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay. Further south and east, the Great Southern is a vast, thinly planted region of granite hills and karri forest whose Riesling, Shiraz and Cabernet are cool, precise and underpriced.
regions.history: Vines arrived with Perth's first settlers in 1829; Olive Farm (1830), Houghton (1836) and Sandalford (1840) on the Swan River made the colony's wine for more than a century, including Jack Mann's Houghton White Burgundy (1937). The south-west was opened by research: Harold Olmo's 1956 report on the Great Southern and John Gladstones' 1965 paper on Margaret River, after which doctors and farmers planted Forest Hill (1966), Vasse Felix (1967), Plantagenet (1968), Moss Wood (1969), Cullen and Cape Mentelle (early 1970s) and Leeuwin (1974).
regions.terroir: A Mediterranean climate with a strong maritime influence: Margaret River is surrounded by ocean on three sides, with almost no frost and very little summer rain (about 210 mm October to April). The Great Southern is cooler (about 1,735 growing degree days) and continental at Frankland River, maritime at Albany and Denmark. Soils are ancient: lateritic gravels over granite and gneiss in Margaret River, granite-derived loams around the Porongurup Range.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Shiraz, Riesling, Merlot, Chenin Blanc (Swan Valley) and Verdelho.
regions.styles: Structured Cabernet and Bordeaux blends, mineral Chardonnay, Semillon-Sauvignon Blanc blends, peppery Great Southern Shiraz, dry Riesling; fortified Verdelho and 'Liqueur' wines in the Swan Valley.
regions.classification: Zones: Greater Perth, South West Australia, Central Western Australia, West Australian South East Coastal and Eastern Plains, Inland and North of Western Australia. Subregions: Swan Valley, and Albany, Denmark, Frankland River, Mount Barker and Porongurup in the Great Southern. Margaret River's six 'Gladstones' subregions (Yallingup, Carbunup, Wilyabrup, Treeton, Wallcliffe, Karridale) are informal.

regions.name: Tasmania
regions.tagline: One GI, seven valleys and Australia's coolest climate: the island that became the country's sparkling and Pinot Noir engine.
regions.summary:
Tasmania is a single GI (it is simultaneously a state, zone and region) with about 1,700 hectares of vines, under 1 percent of Australian wine by volume but a much larger share by value. With fewer than 800 growing degree days on Wine Australia's measure, it is the coolest place in Australia to ripen grapes, and its traditional-method sparkling wine (Jansz, Arras, Clover Hill, House of Arras) and Pinot Noir are the most sought after in the country. Big mainland companies buy Tasmanian fruit for their best fizz.

Wine Tasmania promotes seven informal areas: Tamar Valley, Pipers River, North West, East Coast, Coal River Valley, Derwent Valley and Huon Valley/D'Entrecasteaux Channel. None is a registered GI, but the differences between them (Pipers River's maritime cool, the warm, dry rain shadow of the Coal River and East Coast) are real.
regions.history: Tasmanian cuttings helped found Victoria's and South Australia's vineyards in the 1830s, but the island's own industry faded by the 1860s. The revival began with Jean Miguet's La Provence (1956, now Providence) near Launceston and Claudio Alcorso's Moorilla (1958) on the Derwent. Andrew Pirie's Pipers Brook (1974) proved the north-east; Louis Roederer's partnership at Jansz (1985) and Ed Carr's House of Arras made the island famous for sparkling.
regions.terroir: Cool, maritime and windy, with long autumns. The north (Tamar and Pipers River) is wetter; the south-east (Coal River and Derwent valleys) and East Coast lie in a rain shadow and are among the driest parts of the state. Soils include basalt-derived red earths at Pipers River, dolerite and sandstone in the south, and alluvial gravels.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir (about half the vineyard), Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris and Riesling.
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling (often long lees-aged), Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling.
regions.classification: Single GI 'Tasmania' (registered 1994 on Wine Australia's data). Informal sub-areas are used on labels as place names only where they are not misleading.

regions.name: Queensland
regions.tagline: A tropical state whose wine lives up on the granite, a kilometre above sea level.
regions.summary: Queensland's wine is concentrated in the Granite Belt around Stanthorpe, on the New South Wales border, where altitudes of 600 to 1,300 m give one of the coolest climates in mainland Australia despite a latitude of 28 to 29 degrees south. The South Burnett, north-west of Brisbane, is the other registered region. The state's GI 'Queensland' also functions as a zone.
regions.history: Italian immigrants planted table grapes and some wine grapes around Ballandean in the 1920s and 1930s; Ballandean Estate traces its vines to 1932. A boutique industry grew from the 1960s and 1970s, and the Granite Belt's 'Strange Birds' trail now promotes uncommon varieties.
regions.terroir: Granite-derived sandy soils, frost risk in spring and summer rain from the subtropics.
regions.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Verdelho, Semillon and many alternative varieties (Fiano, Vermentino, Tempranillo, Nebbiolo, Saperavi).
regions.classification: Zone/State GI Queensland; regions Granite Belt and South Burnett.

Wine Australia Open Data Hub, Wine Geographical Indications Australia (feature service with registration year, vine area, climate and crush 2020-2026)

au-adelaide.name: Adelaide
au-adelaide.summary: A 'super zone' wrapping the Mount Lofty Ranges, Fleurieu and Barossa zones, created so that wines blended across the hills and plains near the city can carry a place name more specific than South Australia. It is used mainly for multi-regional blends; its value is that it guarantees the fruit is from the cooler, older vineyards near the capital rather than the irrigated Riverland.
au-adelaide.terroir: Includes everything from Barossa's valley floor to the Adelaide Hills at 700 m and the coastal Fleurieu.
au-adelaide.nerd_note: Adelaide is the only super zone inside a single state; South Eastern Australia, the other super zone, straddles five.

au-adelaide-hills.name: Adelaide Hills
au-adelaide-hills.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Shiraz, Pinot Gris, Grüner Veltliner, Nebbiolo
au-adelaide-hills.summary:
A long, narrow region of hills, orchards and stringybark forest running about 70 km along the Mount Lofty Ranges east of Adelaide. Vineyards sit at roughly 300 to 700 m, which makes it one of the coolest regions in mainland South Australia, and it has become the state's centre for Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, cool-climate Shiraz and traditional-method sparkling.

German settlers planted vines at Hahndorf and Lobethal in the nineteenth century, but by the 1930s the Hills were orchard country. The modern era began with Brian Croser's Petaluma, whose Piccadilly Valley Chardonnay (from 1976 onward) and Croser sparkling proved the site, followed by Henschke at Lenswood, Stephen George's Ashton Hills (Pinot Noir) and Shaw + Smith, whose 1989 Sauvignon Blanc became a benchmark. In the 2000s and 2010s the Basket Range area became the heart of Australia's natural-wine movement, with Lucy Margaux, BK Wines, Ochota Barrels and Commune of Buttons making skin-contact whites, light reds and pét-nats.
au-adelaide-hills.terroir: About 1,710 growing degree days on Wine Australia's data, with 740 mm of annual rain, more than the Barossa or McLaren Vale. Soils are mostly ancient sandstones, schist, quartzite and siltstone, often weathered to grey-brown loam over clay. The northern end (Gumeracha, Birdwood) is warmer; the central Piccadilly Valley and Lenswood are the coolest and wettest.
au-adelaide-hills.nerd_note: Hahndorf Hill planted Grüner Veltliner in 2006 from Austrian clones imported through quarantine, and the Hills now grow most of Australia's Grüner.

au-adelaide-plains.name: Adelaide Plains
au-adelaide-plains.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Colombard, Nero d'Avola
au-adelaide-plains.summary: Flat, hot market-garden country north of Adelaide around Virginia and Angle Vale, registered in 2002. Much of the fruit goes into blends, but Primo Estate (Joe Grilli, who first made Colombard famous here and created the amarone-style Joseph Moda) and Ceravolo show the region can make characterful wine.
au-adelaide-plains.terroir: About 2,250 growing degree days and under 400 mm of annual rain; flat alluvial soils near Gulf St Vincent, irrigated.
au-adelaide-plains.nerd_note: Primo Estate's Joseph Moda Cabernet Merlot uses partially dried grapes, an Australian take on the Veneto's appassimento.

au-albany.name: Albany
au-albany.summary: Maritime vineyards around Western Australia's oldest European settlement (1826), registered in 1999, suited to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Albany's ocean breezes and granite-derived soils give some of Western Australia's most delicate Pinot Noir.
au-albany.terroir: Sandy gravels over granite; strong ocean influence.
au-albany.nerd_note: Wignalls was one of the first to show Western Australian Pinot Noir in the 1980s.

au-alpine-valleys.name: Alpine Valleys
au-alpine-valleys.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Tempranillo, Prosecco, Shiraz, Saperavi
au-alpine-valleys.summary: The Ovens, Kiewa, Buckland and Buffalo river valleys around Bright and Myrtleford, registered in 1999, with vineyards up to about 1,000 m among former tobacco and hop farms. Producers such as Billy Button, Mayford and Gapsted experiment widely.
au-alpine-valleys.terroir: About 1,580 growing degree days; alluvial soils; cold winters.

au-australia.name: Australia
au-australia.summary: The national GI, used for wines blended from anywhere in the country. Most Australian wine sold in casks or at entry-level prices is labelled 'South Eastern Australia' rather than 'Australia', because that super zone already covers the irrigated heartland.

au-australian-capital-territory.name: Australian Capital Territory
au-australian-capital-territory.summary: A state-level GI for the national capital territory. Most 'Canberra District' wineries are across the border in New South Wales; a handful, such as Mount Majura, are inside the ACT.

au-barossa.name: Barossa
au-barossa.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Riesling, Semillon
au-barossa.summary: The Barossa zone joins the warm valley floor of the Barossa Valley with the cooler, higher Eden Valley to the east. Wines labelled simply 'Barossa' are usually blends across both, a historic practice: Barossa winemakers have long balanced the density of valley-floor Shiraz with the acidity and perfume of Eden Valley fruit. The two regions share a history of Silesian settlement, Lutheran churches and family growers whose names (Hoffmann, Kalleske, Lindner, Henschke) recur on labels and vineyard registers.
au-barossa.terroir: A single zone of about 1,690 square kilometres with 13,500 ha of vines, rising from about 110 m on the North Para River to over 600 m on the Barossa Range.
au-barossa.nerd_note: The Barossa Old Vine Charter applies across the zone, so an Ancestor vineyard (125 years or older) can be in either the valley or Eden Valley.

au-barossa-valley.name: Barossa Valley
au-barossa-valley.grapes: Shiraz (about half the vineyard), Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Mourvèdre (Mataro), Semillon, Riesling
au-barossa-valley.summary:
The Barossa Valley is the heartland of Australian Shiraz and holds some of the oldest producing vines on earth. A shallow valley 25 km long, drained by the North Para River 60 km north-east of Adelaide, it was settled from 1842 by Lutheran farmers from Prussian Silesia, who called it 'Neu-Schlesien'. They planted mixed farms with a few rows of vines; when the fortified-wine boom came in the late nineteenth century the vines became the crop. Because South Australia kept phylloxera out, many of those own-rooted, dry-grown bush vines still crop: Langmeil's Freedom Shiraz (1843), Cirillo's Grenache at Light Pass (1848), Turkey Flat's Shiraz at Bethany, Hewitson's Old Garden Mourvèdre (1853) and Penfolds' Block 42 Cabernet at Kalimna (1888).

For decades this fruit went into fortified wine and then into anonymous blends; in the 1980s, with a government vine-pull scheme paying growers to grub up old vines, much was lost. Peter Lehmann, who guaranteed to buy growers' grapes during the crisis, Robert O'Callaghan at Rockford and Charlie Melton saved what remained, and in the 1990s American critics fell for the ripe, dense, chocolate-and-blackberry style. Since the 2010s the style has moved toward earlier picking, less new oak and more whole-bunch Grenache and Mataro, without losing the region's generosity.

The Barossa Old Vine Charter registers vines by age (Old 35+, Survivor 70+, Centenarian 100+, Ancestor 125+). The Barossa Grounds project grouped the valley's soils and climates into broad zones (commonly called the Northern Grounds around Moppa, Ebenezer and Greenock, which give the darkest, most tannic Shiraz; the Central Grounds around Marananga, Seppeltsfield and Tanunda; the warmer, sandier Southern Grounds around Rowland Flat and Lyndoch; and the cooler Eastern Edge and Western Ridge), which producers now cite on labels as informal sub-districts.
au-barossa-valley.terroir: Warm and dry: Wine Australia records about 1,970 growing degree days and 209 mm of growing-season rain, so most of the oldest vines are dry-grown and rely on deep soils that hold winter rain. Soils change over short distances, from red-brown clay loams and ironstone in the north and west (Marananga, Greenock, Ebenezer) to deep sand over clay at Light Pass and Vine Vale and grey sandy loams in the south. Altitude runs from about 110 m on the valley floor to almost 600 m on the western ridge.
au-barossa-valley.nerd_note: Penfolds' Block 42 at Kalimna, planted around 1888, is thought to be the oldest continuously producing Cabernet Sauvignon vineyard in the world; it is bottled alone only in exceptional years.

au-beechworth.name: Beechworth
au-beechworth.summary: A gold-rush town in the foothills of the Victorian Alps that became a cult wine region thanks to Rick Kinzbrunner, who planted Giaconda at Everton Upper in 1982. Giaconda's Chardonnay, fermented with wild yeast and aged in a granite cave cellar, is one of Australia's most sought-after whites, and Kinzbrunner's Nebbiolo and Shiraz are equally serious. Sorrenberg (1985), Castagna (biodynamic Syrah and Sangiovese), Savaterre and A. Rodda followed.
au-beechworth.terroir: About 1,720 growing degree days. Altitudes from about 200 to 1,000 m, on granite and on sandy, quartz-rich soils over decomposed granite; cool nights.
au-beechworth.nerd_note: Giaconda blasted its cellar into the granite hillside so the wines age at a natural cool temperature.

au-bendigo.name: Bendigo
au-bendigo.summary: Gold-rush Bendigo had more than 100 vineyards by 1880 until phylloxera arrived in 1893 and the government ordered vineyards destroyed. Stuart Anderson revived it at Balgownie in 1969, and the region now makes rich, minty Shiraz and Cabernet from small family producers.
au-bendigo.terroir: Warm and dry (about 1,880 growing degree days, 496 mm of rain), on gravelly quartz soils over clay.

au-big-rivers.name: Big Rivers
au-big-rivers.summary: The irrigation zone of inland New South Wales, containing the Riverina, Perricoota, and the New South Wales parts of Murray Darling and Swan Hill. It crushes about a fifth of Australia's grapes.

au-blackwood-valley.name: Blackwood Valley
au-blackwood-valley.summary: An inland valley around Bridgetown and Boyup Brook, registered in 1998, whose fruit is mostly sold to other regions' wineries. Warmer and drier than Pemberton, it suits Shiraz and Cabernet.

au-broke-fordwich.name: Broke Fordwich
au-broke-fordwich.summary: A subregion of the Lower Hunter around Broke, west of Pokolbin, registered in 1997, known for Semillon from sandy creek flats (Wollombi Brook) and for Hunter Semillon from producers such as Margan.
au-broke-fordwich.terroir: Sandy alluvial soils and some volcanic clay; slightly drier than Pokolbin.

au-canberra-district.name: Canberra District
au-canberra-district.summary: A cool, high region around the national capital, most of whose vineyards lie across the border in New South Wales, around Murrumbateman, because land in the Australian Capital Territory is leasehold. Scientists from the CSIRO founded it: John Kirk at Clonakilla (1971) and Edgar Riek at Lake George (1971). Tim Kirk's Clonakilla Shiraz Viognier, co-fermented in the Côte-Rôtie manner since 1992, is one of Australia's most admired wines, and the region's Riesling is fine and dry.
au-canberra-district.terroir: About 1,650 growing degree days; elevations of 500 to 850 m; continental with frosty winters and dry summers; granite and shale soils.
au-canberra-district.nerd_note: Ken Helm organises the annual Canberra International Riesling Challenge.

au-central-ranges.name: Central Ranges
au-central-ranges.summary: The zone on the western slopes and tablelands of the Great Dividing Range, containing Mudgee, Orange and Cowra. The zone's regions climb from about 300 m at Cowra to more than 1,000 m on the slopes of Mount Canobolas at Orange, giving a range of climates for Chardonnay, Shiraz and Cabernet.

au-central-victoria.name: Central Victoria
au-central-victoria.summary: The zone of central Victorian goldfields and river country, containing Bendigo, Heathcote, Goulburn Valley (with Nagambie Lakes), Strathbogie Ranges and Upper Goulburn. Its regions share a gold-rush history: most nineteenth-century vineyards here were planted with mining wealth and destroyed by phylloxera, and the modern industry began again in the 1960s and 1970s.

au-central-western-australia.name: Central Western Australia
au-central-western-australia.summary: A wheatbelt zone east of Perth with about 40 ha of vines and no regions. Its scattered vineyards are mostly hobby or cellar-door plantings among wheat farms.

au-clare-valley.name: Clare Valley
au-clare-valley.grapes: Riesling, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Semillon, Malbec
au-clare-valley.summary:
The Clare Valley, 120 km north of Adelaide, is not one valley but a series of narrow north-south valleys on a plateau between about 300 and 500 m, and it is Australia's most famous source of dry Riesling. Clare Riesling is bone dry, smells of lime juice and lime blossom when young, and turns to toast, honey and kerosene over ten to twenty years. The region also makes structured Shiraz and Cabernet, from estates such as Wendouree and Jim Barry, that need years to soften.

Settlement was varied: the Austrian Jesuits founded Sevenhill in 1851 to make altar wine (they still do), Polish immigrants settled the Polish Hill River valley from 1856, and English and Cornish miners worked the copper mines at nearby Burra. Two sub-areas define Clare Riesling. Watervale, in the south, has red-brown loam over limestone and gives more floral, generous, earlier-drinking wines; Polish Hill, in a side valley to the east, has hard slate and shale and gives austere, tightly wound wines that need time.

Clare also changed how the world closes bottles. In August 2000, fourteen producers including Grosset, Mount Horrocks, Taylors, Leasingham, Mitchell and Knappstein announced they would bottle Riesling together under screwcap, with bottles from Saverglass and caps from Pechiney, because cork taint was ruining at least one bottle in twenty. It worked: aromatic Riesling ages slowly and predictably under screwcap, and within a decade most of Australia and New Zealand had switched.
au-clare-valley.terroir: Wine Australia records about 1,950 growing degree days, warmer than its reputation suggests, but cool nights, altitude and afternoon breezes preserve acidity. Soils are a patchwork: terra rossa and red loam over limestone at Watervale and Auburn, slate and shale at Polish Hill, sandy loam around Sevenhill and Penwortham.
au-clare-valley.nerd_note: Jim Barry's Florita vineyard at Watervale was bought from Leo Buring in 1986; John Vickery's Leo Buring Rieslings made from it in the 1960s and 1970s are among the oldest Australian Rieslings still drinking well.

au-coonawarra.name: Coonawarra
au-coonawarra.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon (more than half the vineyard), Shiraz, Merlot, Chardonnay
au-coonawarra.summary:
Coonawarra is Australia's most famous Cabernet Sauvignon region, and its fame rests on a strip of soil. A narrow band of bright red terra rossa over soft white limestone, about 15 km long and rarely more than 2 km wide, runs north from Penola across flat country otherwise covered by black, poorly drained clays. Vines on the red strip ripen Cabernet with intense blackcurrant fruit, a mint and eucalyptus lift and firm but fine tannins.

The district was invented by John Riddoch, a Scottish pastoralist who in 1890 subdivided part of his property into small blocks for his Penola Fruit Colony and in 1891 built a stone winery with three gables. Bill Redman made the wine from 1901 and kept Coonawarra going through the lean decades; in 1951 the Wynn family bought Riddoch's winery and launched Wynns Coonawarra Estate, whose triple-gabled label is still the region's emblem. Mildara, Lindemans, Penfolds and others followed in the 1960s and 1970s.

Because the soil made the name, the boundary became a decade-long legal fight in the 1990s and early 2000s, as growers on black soil, those just outside and those on the terra rossa argued over what Coonawarra meant. The final boundary (registered in 2003) is broader than the red strip, so the best producers name the soil and the vineyard. The region's water table is high, so vines need little irrigation and suffer little from drought, but spring frost is a real risk.
au-coonawarra.terroir: Cool for its latitude: Wine Australia records about 1,570 growing degree days and a mean January temperature near 20.6 degrees C. Terra rossa (iron-rich red clay loam 20 to 50 cm deep) sits on calcrete and porous limestone; outside the strip are rendzina black soils and sandy flats. Altitude barely varies (about 50 to 130 m).
au-coonawarra.nerd_note: Wynns made its first Black Label Cabernet Sauvignon in 1954; the flagship John Riddoch Cabernet, named after the founder, followed with the 1982 vintage.

au-cowra.name: Cowra
au-cowra.summary: Lower and warmer than Orange, Cowra made its name in the 1970s and 1980s supplying Chardonnay to Petaluma and Rothbury; today its fruit goes mostly into blends. Its warm climate and granite soils give ripe, peachy Chardonnay.
au-cowra.terroir: About 2,250 growing degree days; granite-derived sandy soils along the Lachlan River.
au-cowra.nerd_note: Petaluma's first Chardonnay (1977) used Cowra fruit before Brian Croser planted the Piccadilly Valley.

au-currency-creek.name: Currency Creek
au-currency-creek.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
au-currency-creek.summary: A small region near Goolwa and the Murray Mouth, registered in 2001, with vineyards planted mostly since the 1990s. Its maritime climate and sandy soils give fruit-forward reds and fresh whites, much of it sold to larger wineries.
au-currency-creek.terroir: Close to Lake Alexandrina and the Southern Ocean; about 1,870 growing degree days and 460 mm of rain.
au-currency-creek.nerd_note: The region's name comes from a creek named in 1837 after the cutter 'Currency Lass'.

au-denmark.name: Denmark
au-denmark.summary: The wettest and coolest corner of the Great Southern, among karri and tingle forests near the coast, registered in 2003; Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are the focus. Its high rainfall and cool summers make it the most Burgundian of the Great Southern's subregions.

au-eastern-plains-inland-and-north-of-we.name: Eastern Plains, Inland and North of Western Australia
au-eastern-plains-inland-and-north-of-we.summary: A catch-all zone covering more than two million square kilometres of desert and tropics, from the Kimberley to the Nullarbor, created so that every part of the state sits in a zone.
au-eastern-plains-inland-and-north-of-we.nerd_note: It is by far the largest wine GI in Australia by area, and among the largest in the world.

au-eden-valley.name: Eden Valley
au-eden-valley.grapes: Riesling, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Viognier
au-eden-valley.summary:
Eden Valley is the high, cool eastern half of the Barossa: rolling granite and schist country at 400 to 600 m, with gum trees, sheep paddocks and widely spaced vineyards. It makes two of Australia's greatest wines. Its Riesling is fine, floral and lime-scented, more delicate than Clare's and capable of decades in bottle (Pewsey Vale, Heggies, Henschke Julius, Mesh). And its old Shiraz, above all Henschke's Hill of Grace and Mount Edelstone, shows that Australian Shiraz can be about perfume, spice and silk rather than weight.

Settlement began in the 1840s: Joseph Gilbert planted Pewsey Vale in 1847, and Johann Christian Henschke, a Silesian, started making wine at Keyneton in 1868. The Hill of Grace vineyard, named after the Gnadenberg (Hill of Grace) Lutheran church opposite, holds Shiraz planted in the 1860s; Cyril Henschke first bottled it alone with the 1958 vintage, a pioneering single-vineyard release. Yalumba revived Eden Valley Riesling and planted Viognier there in 1980, one of the first serious plantings in the New World.
au-eden-valley.terroir: About 1,800 growing degree days on Wine Australia's measure, but cold nights and wind make it feel cooler than the figure. Soils are thin and stony, derived from weathered granite, schist, ironstone and quartz, giving low yields. Altitude runs from about 220 m to over 630 m.
au-eden-valley.nerd_note: The 'Grandfathers' in Hill of Grace are Shiraz vines planted in the 1860s by Nicolaus Stanitzki; Henschke propagates new plantings from them using its own massal selection.

au-far-north.name: Far North
au-far-north.summary: A vast zone covering the north of South Australia, from the Flinders Ranges to the deserts, whose only region is the Southern Flinders Ranges. Almost all of its 858,000 square kilometres are desert with no vines.

au-fleurieu.name: Fleurieu
au-fleurieu.summary: The zone covering the Fleurieu Peninsula south of Adelaide and Kangaroo Island. It includes McLaren Vale, Langhorne Creek, Currency Creek, Southern Fleurieu and Kangaroo Island, and together these crush around 15,000 hectares' worth of fruit, much of it red.
au-fleurieu.terroir: Strong maritime influence from Gulf St Vincent, the Southern Ocean and Lake Alexandrina.
au-fleurieu.nerd_note: Langhorne Creek's high yields make the Fleurieu one of the biggest-volume zones outside the irrigated inland.

au-frankland-river.name: Frankland River
au-frankland-river.summary: The most inland and continental part of the Great Southern, registered in 2000, among sheep paddocks and jarrah forest. Frankland Estate's Isolation Ridge Riesling and peppery Shiraz from Alkoomi and Ferngrove show its brightness and spice.
au-frankland-river.terroir: Lateritic gravels and loams; warm days and cold nights; about 1,320 ha of vines.
au-frankland-river.nerd_note: Frankland Estate hosts an international Riesling tasting that has brought Germany's top growers to Western Australia.

au-geelong.name: Geelong
au-geelong.summary: Geelong was one of Australia's biggest wine districts in the 1860s and 1870s, planted by Swiss vignerons, and it was where phylloxera was found in 1877: the government ordered the vines uprooted, and the region vanished for 90 years. Revived from 1966 by Daryl and Nini Sefton at Idyll, it now makes some of Victoria's most distinctive Pinot, Chardonnay and Shiraz, from Gary Farr's By Farr and Bannockburn on the Moorabool Valley's limestone and basalt, and from the Bellarine Peninsula and Surf Coast.
au-geelong.terroir: Dry and windy (518 mm a year), with about 1,570 growing degree days. Three sub-areas: the Moorabool Valley (volcanic basalt and limestone), the Bellarine Peninsula (maritime) and the Surf Coast.
au-geelong.nerd_note: Bannockburn's Serré Pinot Noir comes from a close-planted block of about 9,000 vines per hectare, rare in Australia, planted on Burgundian lines in 1984.

au-geographe.name: Geographe
au-geographe.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Tempranillo, Sangiovese
au-geographe.summary: Coastal plain and hills around Bunbury and the Ferguson Valley, just north of Margaret River, registered in 1999. Warmer than its neighbour, it suits Shiraz, Tempranillo and Italian varieties; Capel Vale (1974) was its pioneer.
au-geographe.terroir: About 2,030 growing degree days; Tuart sands on the coast, gravelly loams in the hills.

au-gippsland.name: Gippsland
au-gippsland.summary: A zone covering eastern Victoria from Phillip Island to the New South Wales border, with no registered regions and fewer than 200 ha of vines. It is famous for one estate: Bass Phillip, where Phillip Jones planted dense, unirrigated Pinot Noir at Leongatha South from 1979 and made wines that were compared with Burgundy grand crus. Burgundian Jean-Marie Fourrier became a partner in the estate in 2020.
au-gippsland.terroir: South Gippsland is cool and wet, on deep, fertile red soils; East Gippsland is warmer.
au-gippsland.nerd_note: Bass Phillip's Premium Pinot comes from vines planted at about 9,000 per hectare, very dense by Australian standards.

au-glenrowan.name: Glenrowan
au-glenrowan.grapes: Shiraz, Durif, Muscat, Muscadelle, Cabernet Sauvignon
au-glenrowan.summary: Ned Kelly's last stand took place at Glenrowan in 1880, and Baileys of Glenrowan, founded in 1870, still makes thick, dry-grown Shiraz and fortified Muscat and Topaque on the red granite soils of the Warby Ranges.
au-glenrowan.terroir: Warm (about 2,020 growing degree days), on deep red loam derived from granite.
au-glenrowan.nerd_note: Baileys' 1920s Block Shiraz is still dry-grown.

au-goulburn-valley.name: Goulburn Valley
au-goulburn-valley.summary: The Goulburn River valley in north-central Victoria, from Seymour to Shepparton. Its heart is the Nagambie Lakes subregion, where Tahbilk has made wine since 1860; elsewhere irrigated orchards dominate. The broader region outside Nagambie Lakes is mostly irrigated orchard and dairy country, with vineyards that supply fruit for larger wineries.
au-goulburn-valley.terroir: Warm (about 2,100 growing degree days) and dry, on alluvial soils.

au-grampians.name: Grampians
au-grampians.grapes: Shiraz, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Meunier
au-grampians.summary: The region around the sandstone Grampians ranges, Ararat and Great Western, whose cool, peppery, medium-bodied Shiraz is among Australia's most elegant. Its history is gold-rush: Henry Best planted Concongella in 1866, and Hans Irvine's Great Western winery (later Seppelt) dug kilometres of tunnels ('drives') to age traditional-method sparkling wine from 1868 onward. Mount Langi Ghiran, Best's and The Story make the reference Shiraz today.
au-grampians.terroir: About 1,540 growing degree days; altitudes up to about 500 m on vineyards; soils of sandy loam over clay and granite-derived gravels.
au-grampians.nerd_note: Seppelt's Great Western also made sparkling Shiraz, a uniquely Australian style, from the 1890s.

au-granite-belt.name: Granite Belt
au-granite-belt.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Verdelho, Fiano, Tempranillo, Saperavi
au-granite-belt.summary: A plateau of granite boulders around Stanthorpe and Ballandean on the New South Wales border, at 600 to 1,300 m, registered in 2002. The altitude makes it cool despite a latitude of 28 to 29 degrees south. Italian migrants grew grapes here from the 1920s; today about 300 ha support boutique wineries, and the 'Strange Birds' trail promotes unusual varieties.
au-granite-belt.terroir: Decomposed granite sands; about 1,880 growing degree days; summer rain and spring frost.

au-great-southern.name: Great Southern
au-great-southern.grapes: Riesling, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir
au-great-southern.summary: Australia's largest wine region by area (about 150 km by 100 km) and one of its least known, the Great Southern covers granite hills, karri forest and coast in the far south-west. Its five subregions (Albany, Denmark, Frankland River, Mount Barker and Porongurup) range from maritime to continental, so the region can make both pristine Riesling and spicy Shiraz. It was the first part of the south-west to be planted for fine wine: after Harold Olmo of UC Davis recommended it in 1956, the state government planted a trial vineyard at Forest Hill near Mount Barker in 1966, and Forest Hill's 1975 Riesling won national trophies.
au-great-southern.terroir: About 1,735 growing degree days, cool and dry in summer. Soils are mostly sandy and gravelly loams over granite, gneiss and laterite.
au-great-southern.nerd_note: Alkoomi, at Frankland River, was planted in 1971 by Merv and Judy Lange on a sheep farm.

au-great-western.name: Great Western
au-great-western.summary: A subregion of the Grampians registered in 2007 around the village of Great Western. Its name had long been used on cheap sparkling wine made elsewhere by Seppelt, and its registration came with legally enforceable conditions on use. It contains Best's Concongella vineyard, planted from 1866, whose Nursery Block holds about 40 varieties, several of them unidentified, and some of the oldest Pinot Meunier and Dolcetto vines in the world.
au-great-western.terroir: Granite-derived sandy loams over clay, cool and dry.
au-great-western.nerd_note: Wine Australia notes that the use of 'Great Western' is subject to legally enforceable conditions because of the history of the name on sparkling wine.

au-greater-perth.name: Greater Perth
au-greater-perth.summary: The zone around Perth, containing the Swan District (with Swan Valley), Perth Hills and Peel. It is where Western Australian wine began in the 1830s, with Olive Farm, Houghton and Sandalford on the Swan River.

au-gundagai.name: Gundagai
au-gundagai.summary: A broad region around Gundagai on the Murrumbidgee, registered in 2002, mostly growing fruit for larger wineries. Its warm western parts grow Shiraz and Cabernet for blends, while higher eastern sites near Tumut are cooler.

au-hastings-river.name: Hastings River
au-hastings-river.summary: A tiny subtropical region around Port Macquarie with about 13 ha of vines, where Cassegrain pioneered Chambourcin in Australia in the 1980s. Its annual rainfall of about 1,450 mm is among the highest of any Australian wine region.

au-heathcote.name: Heathcote
au-heathcote.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Nebbiolo, Fiano
au-heathcote.summary: Heathcote's fame rests on a band of deep red soil derived from Cambrian greenstone, volcanic rock about 500 million years old, that runs north-south along the Mount Camel Range for about 60 km. On it Shiraz is dense yet fresh, with dark fruit, spice and fine tannin. Ron and Elva Laughton planted Jasper Hill in 1975 and their dry-grown, own-rooted Georgia's Paddock and Emily's Paddock Shiraz made the region famous; Wild Duck Creek, Paul Wilson and Tellurian followed. The GI was registered in 2002 after a dispute with Bendigo over the boundary.
au-heathcote.terroir: About 1,880 growing degree days and only 521 mm of annual rain. Altitude 110 to 600 m. The Cambrian red soils hold water well, allowing dry-farming.
au-heathcote.nerd_note: Jasper Hill's Emily's Paddock is co-planted with a little Cabernet Franc, which goes into the Shiraz.

au-henty.name: Henty
au-henty.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon
au-henty.summary: A huge, sparsely planted region in Victoria's far south-west near Portland and Hamilton, one of the coolest in mainland Australia (about 1,430 growing degree days). Crawford River's Rieslings (John Thomson, from 1975) are among the country's best, and Seppelt once sourced Drumborg fruit here for sparkling and Riesling.
au-henty.terroir: Maritime, windy and cool, on volcanic basalt soils near the coast.

au-high-eden.name: High Eden
au-high-eden.summary: The highest part of Eden Valley, registered as a subregion in 2001, around the Barossa Range above Springton and Flaxman Valley. It was championed by David Wynn, who left the family's Wynns business to plant Mountadam here in 1972 and made one of Australia's early cool-climate Chardonnays. Riesling is tight and slow to open; Chardonnay and sparkling base are crisp.
au-high-eden.terroir: Altitudes up to about 630 m, on quartzite, schist and sandy soils, cooler and windier than the rest of Eden Valley.
au-high-eden.nerd_note: At 46 square kilometres, High Eden is one of the smallest registered GIs in Australia.

au-hilltops.name: Hilltops
au-hilltops.summary: Around Young, in cherry country, at 450 to 700 m. A Croatian immigrant, Nichole Jasprizza, planted vines in the 1860s. Today Grove Estate, Freeman and Moppity make firm Shiraz, Cabernet and Nebbiolo.
au-hilltops.terroir: Granite and basalt soils; about 1,975 growing degree days.
au-hilltops.nerd_note: Freeman Vineyards grows Rondinella and Corvina and makes an amarone-style wine.

au-hunter.name: Hunter
au-hunter.summary:
The Hunter is Australia's oldest continuously producing wine region and its most counter-intuitive one. It is too hot, too humid and too wet at harvest for classic viticulture, yet it makes a white that exists nowhere else: Hunter Semillon, picked early at about 10 to 11 percent alcohol, fermented in stainless steel without oak, and bottled lean and lemony. Over ten to twenty years in bottle it develops toast, honey and lanolin flavours that taste as if it had been oaked. Its medium-bodied, earthy Shiraz, once called 'Hunter River Burgundy', is equally individual.

James Busby planted at Kirkton near Branxton around 1830; George Wyndham's Dalwood (1828), Henry Lindeman's Cavendish (1843) and Edward Tyrrell's Ashmans (1858) followed. Maurice O'Shea at Mount Pleasant (1921 to 1956) made the region's greatest mid-century wines, and his sons-in-spirit at Lindemans, Tyrrell's, Drayton's and McWilliam's kept the style alive. Since the 1970s, Lake's Folly (Max Lake's Cabernet, 1963), Brokenwood (Graveyard Shiraz) and the Tyrrells' Vat 1 Semillon and Vat 47 Chardonnay (Australia's first commercial Chardonnay varietal, 1971) have built its modern reputation.

Summer rain and humid cloud cover make the Hunter warm but not baking: the cloud reduces sunshine, and harvest comes early, usually January, to beat the rain. Old, unirrigated vineyards on the red clay of the Brokenback Range (Pokolbin) give the Shiraz; sandy alluvial flats along the creeks give the best Semillon.
au-hunter.terroir: About 2,215 growing degree days but 556 mm of growing-season rain and frequent cloud. Two soil types matter: friable sandy alluvial flats (Semillon) and red-brown volcanic and limestone-derived clay loams on the slopes of the Brokenback Range (Shiraz).
au-hunter.nerd_note: Tyrrell's 4 Acres Shiraz comes from vines planted in 1879; the Old Patch block dates to 1867.

au-hunter-valley.name: Hunter Valley
au-hunter-valley.summary: The zone containing the Hunter region and its subregions. 'Hunter Valley' is the zone's registered name, while the region inside it is simply 'Hunter'; on labels both are used. Its history goes back to James Busby's and George Wyndham's plantings around 1830, and it is the only zone in New South Wales with registered subregions.
au-hunter-valley.nerd_note: The zone 'Hunter Valley' and the region 'Hunter' have almost identical boundaries.

au-kangaroo-island.name: Kangaroo Island
au-kangaroo-island.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
au-kangaroo-island.summary: Australia's third-largest island, 13 km off the Fleurieu Peninsula, has about 144 ha of vines spread among small family producers. The bushfires of December 2019 and January 2020 burnt about half the island and damaged several vineyards.
au-kangaroo-island.terroir: Cool and maritime (about 1,625 growing degree days), with laterite and ironstone soils.
au-kangaroo-island.nerd_note: The Islander Estate was founded by Jacques Lurton of the Bordeaux family.

au-king-valley.name: King Valley
au-king-valley.grapes: Prosecco (Glera), Pinot Grigio, Sangiovese, Nebbiolo, Chardonnay, Riesling
au-king-valley.summary: A narrow valley rising into the Alps from Milawa, settled after the Second World War by Italian families who grew tobacco. When tobacco collapsed in the 1990s they planted vines, and the Pizzini, Dal Zotto and Brown families made the King Valley Australia's Prosecco capital. Otto Dal Zotto planted the first Prosecco vines in 1999. Since an EU challenge, Australia has defended 'Prosecco' as a grape variety name. Brown Brothers, founded at Milawa in 1889, is the region's oldest producer.
au-king-valley.terroir: Vineyards from about 150 m at Milawa to over 800 m at Whitlands; about 1,710 growing degree days, wetter (970 mm) than most.
au-king-valley.nerd_note: Brown Brothers runs a small 'Kindergarten' winery where it has trialled more than 100 grape varieties.

au-langhorne-creek.name: Langhorne Creek
au-langhorne-creek.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Merlot, Malbec, Chardonnay
au-langhorne-creek.summary:
A flat, quiet region on the floodplains of the Bremer and Angas rivers near Lake Alexandrina, and one of Australia's great unsung sources of soft, fleshy red. It has about 6,100 ha of vines, more than McLaren Vale's area of land would suggest, and much of its fruit disappears into famous blends: Wolf Blass's Black Label and many big-company Cabernet Shiraz blends rely on it.

Frank Potts founded Bleasdale here in 1850 and the family still runs it; Potts cut red gum from the riverbanks to build a huge lever press that still stands. Growers historically flooded their vineyards in winter by diverting the rivers, and the 'Lake Doctor', an afternoon breeze off Lake Alexandrina, cools ripening fruit. Saltram's Metala vineyard dates from 1891.
au-langhorne-creek.terroir: Low-lying (under 65 m), with deep alluvial sandy loams over clay. About 1,970 growing degree days but only 389 mm of annual rain, so water from the lake and rivers matters.
au-langhorne-creek.nerd_note: Bleasdale's red gum lever press, built in 1892 from a single tree trunk, worked until 1960 and is still on site.

au-lenswood.name: Lenswood
au-lenswood.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling
au-lenswood.summary: A high, apple-growing valley in the central Adelaide Hills, registered in 1998 as one of Australia's first subregions. Henschke's Lenswood vineyard (Croft Chardonnay, Giles Pinot Noir), Knappstein Lenswood and Pike & Joyce showed its Chardonnay and Pinot have the acidity for long ageing.
au-lenswood.terroir: Steep slopes at roughly 400 to 560 m, on podzolic soils over sandstone and schist; cooler and wetter than most of the Hills.
au-lenswood.nerd_note: Lenswood is only about 39 square kilometres, among the smallest GIs in Australia.

au-limestone-coast.name: Limestone Coast
au-limestone-coast.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Merlot, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
au-limestone-coast.summary: The flat south-east corner of South Australia, a former seabed of limestone ridges and swamps that runs from Padthaway to Mount Gambier. Its regions (Coonawarra, Wrattonbully, Padthaway, Mount Benson, Robe and Mount Gambier) share cool maritime air and soils of terra rossa or sand over limestone, and together grow about 15,400 ha of vines.
au-limestone-coast.terroir: Low relief, high water tables and a cool climate moderated by the Southern Ocean.
au-limestone-coast.nerd_note: 'Limestone Coast' on a label often means a blend from Coonawarra, Wrattonbully and Padthaway.

au-lower-murray.name: Lower Murray
au-lower-murray.summary: The zone covering South Australia's stretch of the Murray River, whose only region is the Riverland. It is the largest wine-producing zone in the state by volume. In 2026 the Riverland alone crushed about 389,000 tonnes, close to a third of Australia's harvest, so the zone's fortunes are a barometer of the bulk-wine market.
au-lower-murray.terroir: Hot, dry and irrigated from the Murray.

au-macedon-ranges.name: Macedon Ranges
au-macedon-ranges.summary: The coldest wine region on mainland Australia by Wine Australia's measure (about 1,390 growing degree days), high on the Great Dividing Range north-west of Melbourne around Kyneton, Gisborne, Lancefield and Woodend. It is marginal country, where a cold spring can cut a crop in half, but its traditional-method sparkling and taut Pinot and Chardonnay are among Australia's most elegant. Bindi (Michael Dhillon), Curly Flat, Hanging Rock and Granite Hills are the reference producers.
au-macedon-ranges.terroir: Altitudes of about 300 to 800 m; granite, sandstone and volcanic soils; windy, with frost risk.
au-macedon-ranges.nerd_note: Hanging Rock Winery's 'Macedon' non-vintage sparkling uses a solera-style reserve system started in the late 1980s.

au-manjimup.name: Manjimup
au-manjimup.summary: Forest and orchard country north of Pemberton, registered in 2006, also known for truffles. Its vineyards, at about 100 to 350 m, sit between Pemberton's karri forest and the drier Blackwood Valley, and are known for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Merlot.
au-manjimup.terroir: About 1,740 growing degree days; lateritic gravel loams.
au-manjimup.nerd_note: Manjimup produces most of Australia's black Périgord truffles.

au-margaret-river.name: Margaret River
au-margaret-river.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Shiraz, Merlot
au-margaret-river.summary:
Margaret River is a narrow, wave-beaten cape between the Indian and Southern oceans, 270 km south of Perth, and in barely 50 years it has become one of the world's best regions for Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay. Its existence was predicted on paper. In 1965 the agronomist John Gladstones published an analysis showing that the area's climate resembled Bordeaux in a dry year. Dr Tom Cullity, a Perth cardiologist, planted Vasse Felix in 1967; other doctors followed with Moss Wood (Bill Pannell, 1969) and Cullen (Kevin and Diana Cullen, 1971), then Cape Mentelle (David Hohnen, 1970), Sandalford, Leeuwin Estate (Denis and Tricia Horgan, 1974, with advice from Robert Mondavi) and Voyager.

The Cabernet is the region's signature: ripe, structured and fine-grained, with blackcurrant, bay leaf and a saline freshness, and with remarkable consistency from year to year because the ocean buffers both heat and frost. Chardonnay rivals it: Leeuwin Estate's Art Series Chardonnay, first made in 1980, was the first Australian white to rank with grand cru Burgundy, and the region's distinctive Gingin clone, with its 'hen and chicken' bunches of large and small berries, gives concentrated, pineapple-and-grapefruit wines. Semillon-Sauvignon Blanc blends are the everyday white.

Gladstones later proposed six subregions based on soils and climate: Yallingup, Carbunup, Wilyabrup, Treeton, Wallcliffe and Karridale. They are not registered GIs but are widely used. Wilyabrup, in the north-centre, holds Vasse Felix, Moss Wood, Cullen and Woodlands and is the classic Cabernet district; the southern Wallcliffe and Karridale, cooler and wetter, give finer Chardonnay.
au-margaret-river.terroir: Wine Australia records about 1,900 growing degree days and only 213 mm of rain from October to April against 914 mm for the year. Ocean on three sides prevents frost and extreme heat; strong winds at flowering cut yields. Soils are ancient: gravelly and sandy loams derived from granite and gneiss of the Leeuwin Complex, often lateritic, over clay.
au-margaret-river.nerd_note: Cullen was certified biodynamic in 2004, and its Diana Madeline Cabernet blend is named after founder Di Cullen.

au-mclaren-vale.name: McLaren Vale
au-mclaren-vale.grapes: Shiraz, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Mourvèdre, Fiano, Nero d'Avola, Vermentino, Tempranillo
au-mclaren-vale.summary:
McLaren Vale is a Mediterranean pocket between the Mount Lofty Ranges and Gulf St Vincent, 40 minutes south of Adelaide, and it makes some of Australia's most interesting warm-climate reds. It was planted almost as soon as South Australia was settled: John Reynell put in vines at Reynella in 1838, and Thomas Hardy, who bought Tintara in 1876, built the business that became the country's biggest wine company. Old dry-grown Shiraz and Grenache survive across the region, many over 80 years old.

The style of the region changed after 2000. Shiraz remains the main grape, but Grenache from the deep sands of Blewitt Springs, picked earlier and made with whole bunches, has become its signature: pale, perfumed and fine, from producers such as Yangarra, SC Pannell, Bekkers, Ox Hardy and Clarendon Hills. Hot, dry summers and limited water have pushed growers toward Mediterranean varieties: Coriole was among the first to plant Sangiovese and Fiano, and Fiano, Vermentino, Nero d'Avola, Montepulciano and Tempranillo are spreading. The region also leads Australia in organic and biodynamic certification.

McLaren Vale's growers mapped their geology in 2010 and found around 40 rock and soil units, ranging from recent sands to rocks more than 500 million years old. The region now uses an informal district map with names such as Blewitt Springs, Clarendon, Kangarilla, McLaren Flat, Seaview, Willunga and Sellicks Foothills, so drinkers can tell a sandy, perfumed Blewitt Springs Grenache from a dense, ironstone-grown Seaview Shiraz.
au-mclaren-vale.terroir: About 1,940 growing degree days and only 211 mm of growing-season rain. Afternoon sea breezes off Gulf St Vincent moderate the heat. Soils vary sharply: deep, white-grey sands over clay at Blewitt Springs, ironstone and red clay at Seaview, terra rossa and limestone in the south around Willunga, and older siltstones and quartzites near the hills at Clarendon (up to about 400 m).
au-mclaren-vale.nerd_note: d'Arenberg still uses open fermenters and basket presses for its reds, foot-treading the fruit; in 2017 it opened the d'Arenberg Cube, a five-storey glass Rubik's-cube-shaped cellar door.

au-mornington-peninsula.name: Mornington Peninsula
au-mornington-peninsula.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Shiraz
au-mornington-peninsula.summary: A boot-shaped peninsula between Port Phillip Bay and Western Port, an hour south of Melbourne, surrounded by water on three sides. Vines arrived in the 1880s, but the modern industry dates from the 1970s, when Baillieu Myer (Elgee Park, 1972) and Nat and Rosalie White (Main Ridge, 1975) planted. Today about 200 small vineyards make Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris (often labelled Pinot Grigio in a nod to the peninsula's Italian heritage) with a tense, saline freshness. Producers such as Paringa Estate, Kooyong, Stonier, Yabby Lake, Ten Minutes by Tractor, Eldridge and Moorooduc have built an international reputation for Pinot that varies vineyard by vineyard.
au-mornington-peninsula.terroir: Maritime and cool (about 1,560 growing degree days). Red Hill and Main Ridge, at 150 to 300 m on deep red volcanic soils, are the coolest; Moorooduc and Tuerong, lower and on sandier soils over clay, are warmer and riper. Strong winds at flowering reduce yields.
au-mornington-peninsula.nerd_note: Kathleen Quealy and Kevin McCarthy at T'Gallant made Pinot Grigio fashionable in Australia in the 1990s.

au-mount-barker.name: Mount Barker
au-mount-barker.summary: The first Great Southern subregion (1997) and home of Plantagenet (1968) and Forest Hill (1966), whose early Rieslings and Shiraz established the region. Wines are structured, with peppery Shiraz and long-lived Riesling.
au-mount-barker.terroir: Lateritic gravelly loam over granite and gneiss.

au-mount-benson.name: Mount Benson
au-mount-benson.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay
au-mount-benson.summary: A coastal region near Kingston SE, planted from the late 1980s, notable for investment from the Rhône: Michel Chapoutier planted biodynamic Shiraz here in the late 1990s. The climate is cool and windy, giving peppery Shiraz.
au-mount-benson.terroir: Terra rossa and sand over limestone within sight of the ocean; about 1,520 growing degree days.
au-mount-benson.nerd_note: Chapoutier's Mount Benson vineyard was one of the first biodynamic plantings in South Australia.

au-mount-gambier.name: Mount Gambier
au-mount-gambier.grapes: Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Riesling
au-mount-gambier.summary: South Australia's coolest region, around the extinct volcano and Blue Lake at Mount Gambier, registered in 2010. Small vineyards make crisp whites, Pinot Noir and sparkling base.
au-mount-gambier.terroir: About 1,450 growing degree days, volcanic and limestone soils, frequent cloud and wind.
au-mount-gambier.nerd_note: The Blue Lake in the volcano's crater turns cobalt blue every November.

au-mount-lofty-ranges.name: Mount Lofty Ranges
au-mount-lofty-ranges.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Riesling, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
au-mount-lofty-ranges.summary: The zone that follows the Mount Lofty Ranges north and south of Adelaide, grouping three very different regions: the cool Adelaide Hills, the warm Clare Valley 100 km north, and the flat Adelaide Plains. It is rarely seen on labels; its regions do the work.
au-mount-lofty-ranges.terroir: Elevations rise to over 700 m in the Adelaide Hills; the ranges catch more rain than the plains and the Barossa.
au-mount-lofty-ranges.nerd_note: The Clare Valley sits in this zone, not in the Barossa zone, even though Clare and Barossa are often discussed together.

au-mudgee.name: Mudgee
au-mudgee.summary: Mudgee was planted by German settlers in 1858 and was one of Australia's first regions to adopt a quality-control appellation (a voluntary scheme in 1979). Its Aboriginal name means 'nest in the hills'. Huntington Estate, Lowe and Robert Stein make generous Cabernet and Shiraz; Craigmoor's Chardonnay plantings were among Australia's oldest.
au-mudgee.terroir: Altitudes from about 450 to 1,100 m on the western slopes; warm days and cool nights; red loams over clay.
au-mudgee.nerd_note: Mudgee is thought to have provided one of the clones from which much Australian Chardonnay descends (the 'Mudgee clone').

au-murray-darling.name: Murray Darling
au-murray-darling.grapes: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Colombard
au-murray-darling.summary: One of the three great irrigated regions, straddling the Murray around Mildura, Robinvale and Wentworth in both Victoria and New South Wales, with about 13,500 ha of vines. In 2026 it crushed about 237,000 tonnes. The Chaffey brothers began irrigation at Mildura in 1887. Lindeman's Karadoc winery made the region's best-known export, Bin 65 Chardonnay, launched in 1985; at its peak several million cases a year were sold.
au-murray-darling.terroir: About 2,550 growing degree days and 284 mm of rain a year: entirely irrigated. Sandy red mallee soils.
au-murray-darling.nerd_note: The GI is registered in both Victoria and New South Wales because it crosses the state line along the river.

au-nagambie-lakes.name: Nagambie Lakes
au-nagambie-lakes.grapes: Shiraz, Marsanne, Cabernet Sauvignon, Viognier, Roussanne
au-nagambie-lakes.summary: A subregion registered in 2001, defined by the lagoons and billabongs of the Goulburn River near Nagambie, the only Australian GI defined by its water bodies. It holds Tahbilk, whose 1860 Shiraz block survived phylloxera on sandy soils, and whose Marsanne vineyard (planted from 1927) is one of the largest and oldest in the world. Mitchelton, founded in 1969 with a tower overlooking the river, is the other landmark.
