au-nagambie-lakes.terroir: Wine Australia's description points to the influence of the lakes and the region's red sandy loams with ironstone gravel; the water moderates temperatures at night.
au-nagambie-lakes.nerd_note: Tahbilk's Marsanne is unoaked and built to age: at ten years old it tastes of honeysuckle and lanolin.

au-new-england-australia.name: New England Australia
au-new-england-australia.summary: A high plateau around Armidale, Tenterfield and Inverell, registered in 2008, with vineyards at up to about 1,300 m. The suffix 'Australia' distinguishes it from New England in the United States.
au-new-england-australia.terroir: About 1,760 growing degree days; granite and basalt.

au-new-south-wales.name: New South Wales
au-new-south-wales.summary: The state GI for New South Wales, including the irrigated Riverina and the Hunter. New South Wales crushes the second-largest share of Australia's grapes, most of it from the Riverina around Griffith, and it holds the country's first vineyards (Farm Cove, 1788, and Camden Park).

au-north-east-victoria.name: North East Victoria
au-north-east-victoria.grapes: Muscat, Muscadelle, Shiraz, Durif, Prosecco, Sangiovese
au-north-east-victoria.summary: The zone of the Ovens and King valleys, the Victorian Alps and the Murray around Rutherglen: Rutherglen, Glenrowan, Beechworth, King Valley and Alpine Valleys. The zone is the home of Rutherglen Muscat and Topaque and of the Italian families of the King Valley, and it climbs from the Murray plains to alpine vineyards at almost 1,000 m.

au-north-west-victoria.name: North West Victoria
au-north-west-victoria.grapes: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc
au-north-west-victoria.summary: The Victorian bank of the Murray, from Swan Hill to Mildura. Its regions, Murray Darling and Swan Hill, cross the river into New South Wales. Almost all of its fruit is irrigated from the Murray and goes into branded and bulk wine, much of it labelled South Eastern Australia.

au-northern-rivers.name: Northern Rivers
au-northern-rivers.summary: Subtropical north coast of New South Wales; its only region is Hastings River. Summer rain and humidity make viticulture difficult, which is why disease-resistant hybrids such as Chambourcin are common.

au-northern-slopes.name: Northern Slopes
au-northern-slopes.summary: The northern tablelands and slopes of New South Wales; its only region is New England Australia. Its vineyards are scattered across a cool, high tableland, often above 1,000 m.

au-northern-territory.name: Northern Territory
au-northern-territory.summary: A state-level GI covering the Northern Territory, registered for completeness; there is essentially no commercial viticulture apart from a former vineyard near Alice Springs (Chateau Hornsby, 1970s to 2000s).
au-northern-territory.nerd_note: Chateau Hornsby at Alice Springs was for decades Australia's most remote winery.

au-orange.name: Orange
au-orange.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir
au-orange.summary: Orange is defined by altitude: the GI covers only land above 600 m on the slopes of Mount Canobolas, an extinct volcano reaching 1,395 m. That makes it one of Australia's coolest regions, with crisp Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, elegant Shiraz and Pinot Noir. Philip Shaw, Ross Hill, Printhie, Bloodwood (one of the first, 1983) and See Saw lead.
au-orange.terroir: Basalt-derived red volcanic soils near the mountain, shale and limestone lower down; about 1,620 growing degree days.
au-orange.nerd_note: The 600 m contour line is written into the GI definition.

au-padthaway.name: Padthaway
au-padthaway.grapes: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc
au-padthaway.summary: Planted from the 1960s by Seppelt and Lindemans, who were looking for cheap land with good water and a cool climate, Padthaway (originally called Keppoch) became a major source of Chardonnay for national brands; Hardys' Eileen Hardy Chardonnay long relied on it. Today it supplies Shiraz and Cabernet too, with a few local labels.
au-padthaway.terroir: Terra rossa and sandy loams over limestone, on a low ridge; about 1,700 growing degree days and 480 mm of rain, warmer than Coonawarra.
au-padthaway.nerd_note: Padthaway Estate operates in a former homestead built in 1882 and was one of the first to make traditional-method sparkling in the region.

au-peel.name: Peel
au-peel.summary: A coastal region around Mandurah, registered in 2001, with about 50 ha of vines. Its sandy coastal soils suit Chenin Blanc and Shiraz.
au-peel.nerd_note: Peel Estate held an annual blind 'Shiraz tasting' comparing six-year-old Australian Shiraz, started in the 1980s.

au-pemberton.name: Pemberton
au-pemberton.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Merlot
au-pemberton.summary: Karri-forest country around Pemberton, registered in 2006, cooler and wetter than Margaret River; Picardy (founded by Bill Pannell after he sold Moss Wood) made its reputation for Pinot and Chardonnay.
au-pemberton.terroir: About 1,730 growing degree days, 1,095 mm of rain; karri loam and gravel.

au-perricoota.name: Perricoota
au-perricoota.summary: A small irrigated region near Moama on the Murray, opposite Echuca, registered in 1999. Its warm, flat vineyards along the Murray grow Shiraz, Cabernet and Chardonnay, much of it sold to larger wineries.

au-perth-hills.name: Perth Hills
au-perth-hills.summary: Small vineyards in the Darling Range east of Perth, registered in 1999, cooler than the Swan Valley below. Its elevated sites, on lateritic gravel, get cool evening breezes and ripen grapes later than the Swan Valley.
au-perth-hills.terroir: Lateritic and granitic soils at 150 to 400 m.

au-piccadilly-valley.name: Piccadilly Valley
au-piccadilly-valley.summary: A small, cool valley beneath Mount Lofty, registered in 2000. Brian Croser planted Petaluma's Tiers vineyard here in 1979, and the Tiers Chardonnay (now under Croser's Tapanappa label) is one of Australia's most precise. It is also prime country for sparkling base wine.
au-piccadilly-valley.terroir: Among the highest and wettest vineyards in the Hills, at about 500 to 700 m, on brown loam over clay and sandstone.
au-piccadilly-valley.nerd_note: At about 42 square kilometres with 221 ha of vines, Piccadilly Valley produces less than a single big Riverland vineyard but some of the country's most expensive Chardonnay.

au-pokolbin.name: Pokolbin
au-pokolbin.summary: The historic heart of the Lower Hunter, registered as a subregion in 2010, under the Brokenback Range west of Cessnock. Almost every famous Hunter name is here: Tyrrell's, Mount Pleasant, Lake's Folly, Brokenwood, Drayton's and Tulloch.
au-pokolbin.terroir: Red volcanic and limestone-derived clay loams on the slopes, sandy alluvial flats near the creeks; about 1,355 ha of vines in 173 square kilometres.
au-pokolbin.nerd_note: Mount Pleasant's Lovedale vineyard, planted by O'Shea in 1946, gives one of the Hunter's longest-lived Semillons.

au-porongurup.name: Porongurup
au-porongurup.summary: Vineyards on the north-facing slopes of the Porongurup Range, a granite massif 1.1 billion years old, registered in 1999. Castle Rock and Duke's Vineyard make some of Australia's most delicate, mineral Riesling.
au-porongurup.terroir: Karri loam over decomposed granite at 250 to 400 m, above the frost line; about 96 ha of vines.

au-port-phillip.name: Port Phillip
au-port-phillip.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon
au-port-phillip.summary: The zone around Melbourne and Port Phillip Bay, containing the Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula, Geelong, Macedon Ranges and Sunbury. It is Victoria's cool-climate core and the centre of Australian Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
au-port-phillip.terroir: Bay and Bass Strait moderate the coastal regions; the Great Dividing Range lifts Macedon.

au-pyrenees.name: Pyrenees
au-pyrenees.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay
au-pyrenees.summary: Rolling hills around Avoca and Moonambel, named after the Pyrenees by the explorer Thomas Mitchell. Rémy Martin planted Chateau Remy (now Blue Pyrenees) for brandy and sparkling in 1963, and Taltarni and Dalwhinnie built the reputation for firm, minty Shiraz and Cabernet.
au-pyrenees.terroir: About 1,710 growing degree days; 507 mm of rain; quartz-gravel and clay loams at 200 to 800 m.

au-queensland.name: Queensland
au-queensland.summary: Queensland's state GI, which also acts as its zone. It contains the Granite Belt and South Burnett regions; elsewhere small vineyards grow around Mount Tamborine and the Darling Downs.
au-queensland.terroir: Subtropical; quality vineyards depend on altitude.

au-riverina.name: Riverina
au-riverina.grapes: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Semillon, Cabernet Sauvignon, Durif, Pinot Grigio
au-riverina.summary: The Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area around Griffith and Leeton, opened in 1912 and settled largely by Italian families, crushes about 235,000 to 300,000 tonnes a year. Casella's [yellow tail], launched in 2001, became the best-selling imported wine brand in the United States within a few years. The region's one great wine is a sweet one: De Bortoli's Noble One botrytis Semillon, first made in 1982, showed that the morning humidity around Griffith could produce noble rot in autumn.
au-riverina.terroir: About 2,545 growing degree days, 420 mm of annual rain; flat red loams irrigated from the Murrumbidgee.
au-riverina.nerd_note: De Bortoli Noble One is Australia's most successful sweet table wine; the first 1982 vintage was made from Semillon left on the vine after a sales slump.

au-riverland.name: Riverland
au-riverland.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Merlot, Colombard, Petit Verdot, Nero d'Avola, Montepulciano, Fiano
au-riverland.summary:
The Riverland, along the Murray around Renmark, Berri, Loxton and Waikerie, is Australia's largest wine region by tonnage, with about 21,800 ha of vines. In 2026 it crushed about 389,000 tonnes, roughly 30 percent of the national total, even in a short year. The Canadian Chaffey brothers began irrigation at Renmark in 1887, and soldier-settler blocks after both world wars filled it with family growers. Its fruit makes cask, bulk and branded wine for the world.

The Riverland is also where Australia is rethinking warm-climate wine. Growers such as Ashley Ratcliff (Ricca Terra), 919 Wines, Bassham and Delinquente have planted Nero d'Avola, Montepulciano, Fiano, Vermentino and Touriga Nacional, varieties that hold acidity in the heat and need less water. The falling demand for cheap red since 2020 has hit the region hardest: many growers have left grapes unpicked or pulled out vines.
au-riverland.terroir: Hot and dry: about 2,350 growing degree days, 148 mm of growing-season rain and 254 mm a year. Every vine depends on Murray water allocations. Sandy loams over limestone (mallee country).
au-riverland.nerd_note: Angove's, founded in 1886 near Adelaide, moved to Renmark in 1910 and later invented one of the first commercial wine casks with a tap in the 1960s.

au-robe.name: Robe
au-robe.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir
au-robe.summary: A cool coastal region around the fishing town of Robe, registered in 2006. Large vineyards supply fruit to Treasury Wine Estates and others; local sparkling and Pinot show the climate.
au-robe.terroir: One of the coolest Limestone Coast regions (about 1,485 growing degree days), on limestone ridges and sand.
au-robe.nerd_note: Robe was a landing point for thousands of Chinese gold seekers in the 1850s, who walked from here to the Victorian goldfields to avoid a landing tax.

au-rutherglen.name: Rutherglen
au-rutherglen.grapes: Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge ('Rutherglen Brown Muscat'), Muscadelle, Durif, Shiraz
au-rutherglen.summary:
Rutherglen, on the Murray River in north-east Victoria, makes one of the world's great fortified wines, and it does so from grapes ripened to raisins on the vine. Gold was found here in 1860; the gold ran out within a decade, but many miners stayed and planted vines, and by the 1880s the region was exporting to London. Phylloxera arrived in 1899 and the region shrank, but a handful of families (Chambers, Morris, Campbell, Sutherland Smith at All Saints, Stanton & Killeen) kept their soleras of fortified wine going, some for more than 140 years.

Rutherglen Muscat is made from a dark-skinned clone of Muscat à Petits Grains, left on the vine until the berries shrivel and reach 17 to 20 degrees Baumé. Fermentation is stopped early with grape spirit, and the wine then ages for years in old casks stacked in hot iron sheds, where heat concentrates it and the 'angels' share' takes about half the volume over 20 years. The result is dark brown, viscous and tastes of raisin, toffee, coffee and rose petal. Topaque, made the same way from Muscadelle, was called Tokay until EU agreements retired the name in 2010; it tastes of malt, tea leaf and butterscotch.

The producers' Muscat of Rutherglen network classifies these wines on four tiers by richness and age: Rutherglen (an average age of about 3 to 5 years), Classic (6 to 10), Grand (11 to 19) and Rare (more than 20 years). Only a few hundred bottles of the Rare wines are released each year; Chambers Rosewood and Morris have barrels from the 1890s and earlier in their blends. The region also makes dense, inky Durif, a red grape that found its best Australian home here.
au-rutherglen.terroir: Warm and continental (about 2,080 growing degree days), with hot days, cool nights and a long dry autumn that lets fruit shrivel safely on the vine. Soils are red loams and alluvial sands along the Murray; vineyards sit at about 120 to 590 m.
au-rutherglen.nerd_note: Bill Chambers' blends of Rare Muscat include wine from casks started by his great-grandfather; the oldest material in the Chambers solera is thought to date to the 1890s.

au-shoalhaven-coast.name: Shoalhaven Coast
au-shoalhaven-coast.summary: A humid coastal region around Nowra and Berry, where disease-resistant Chambourcin is a local specialty because summer rain brings mildew. Its small producers sell mostly to visitors from Sydney, and humid summers make disease control the main viticultural task.
au-shoalhaven-coast.nerd_note: Coolangatta Estate stands on the convict-built estate founded by Alexander Berry in the 1820s, now restored as a winery and resort.

au-south-australia.name: South Australia
au-south-australia.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Grenache, Riesling, Merlot
au-south-australia.summary: The state GI covers every vineyard in South Australia and appears on blends drawn from several regions, such as multi-regional Shiraz from the big companies. South Australia crushes roughly half of Australia's grapes, and as a phylloxera-free state with tight quarantine on vine material it holds most of the country's pre-1900 plantings.
au-south-australia.terroir: From the hot, irrigated Riverland to the cool Limestone Coast and the elevated Mount Lofty Ranges; the common thread is winter rainfall and dry summers.
au-south-australia.nerd_note: Vinehealth Australia (originally the Phylloxera Board of South Australia, created under an 1899 act) still controls the movement of vines, used machinery and even grape bins into the state.

au-south-burnett.name: South Burnett
au-south-burnett.summary: A warm, subtropical region around Kingaroy and Murgon, registered in 2000, with small cellar-door wineries. Its summer rainfall and warmth suit Verdelho, Shiraz and hybrid grapes.

au-south-coast.name: South Coast
au-south-coast.summary: The coastal zone south of Sydney, containing Shoalhaven Coast and Southern Highlands. It covers the humid coastal strip and the cooler Southern Highlands behind it, both close enough to Sydney for cellar-door tourism.

au-south-eastern-australia.name: South Eastern Australia
au-south-eastern-australia.grapes: Shiraz, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio, Moscato
au-south-eastern-australia.summary: The super zone that took Australian wine to the world. It covers all of New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania and the wine-growing parts of Queensland and South Australia, and so includes the three great irrigated regions on the Murray, Darling and Murrumbidgee rivers. It lets companies blend fruit freely from Coonawarra to the Riverina and still name a place. Brands such as Jacob's Creek, [yellow tail], Lindeman's Bin 65 and Hardys Stamp built their export volume under this label.
au-south-eastern-australia.terroir: Too large to have a single terroir; it exists for blending.
au-south-eastern-australia.nerd_note: South Eastern Australia was registered in 1996; its boundary in South Australia and Queensland was drawn to exclude deserts and the tropical north.

au-south-west-australia.name: South West Australia
au-south-west-australia.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Shiraz, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon
au-south-west-australia.summary: The zone covering Western Australia's fine-wine heartland: Margaret River, Great Southern, Geographe, Pemberton, Manjimup and Blackwood Valley, with about 9,900 ha of vines. Margaret River alone grows more than half of the zone's vines and crushed about 28,000 tonnes in 2024 and 2025.

au-southern-fleurieu.name: Southern Fleurieu
au-southern-fleurieu.grapes: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir
au-southern-fleurieu.summary: The hilly tip of the Fleurieu Peninsula, from Mount Compass to Cape Jervis and Victor Harbor, registered in 2001. Cooler and wetter than McLaren Vale next door, it suits Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and medium-bodied reds.
au-southern-fleurieu.terroir: About 1,640 growing degree days and 700 mm of annual rain, with Southern Ocean winds.
au-southern-fleurieu.nerd_note: Salomon Estate's founder Bert Salomon is an Austrian winemaker who works vintages in both hemispheres.

au-southern-flinders-ranges.name: Southern Flinders Ranges
au-southern-flinders-ranges.summary: Small vineyards in the hills around Wirrabara, Port Pirie and Laura, registered in 2003, mostly making full, warm-climate reds and some Riesling for local producers. It is the northernmost wine region in South Australia, and its cooler hill sites near Wirrabara and Bundaleer Forest show that altitude can offset the heat of the plains below.
au-southern-flinders-ranges.terroir: Warm (about 2,220 growing degree days) but with cooler pockets at altitude up to about 950 m.

au-southern-highlands.name: Southern Highlands
au-southern-highlands.summary: A cool, wet plateau around Bowral and Moss Vale at 500 to 900 m, two hours south of Sydney, registered in 2002, mostly cellar-door producers. Rain and spring frost are the main risks; Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and sparkling wine make the most of the cool climate.
au-southern-highlands.terroir: About 1,640 growing degree days, 940 mm of rain.

au-southern-new-south-wales.name: Southern New South Wales
au-southern-new-south-wales.summary: The zone containing Canberra District, Hilltops, Tumbarumba and Gundagai. It stretches from the Canberra District's cool, high plateau to Tumbarumba in the Snowy Mountains foothills, and much of its fruit goes to sparkling and premium Chardonnay.

au-strathbogie-ranges.name: Strathbogie Ranges
au-strathbogie-ranges.summary: A granite plateau between the Goulburn Valley and the Upper Goulburn at roughly 150 to 1,000 m, registered in 2002, supplying cool-climate Riesling, Chardonnay and sparkling base as well as some fine Shiraz.
au-strathbogie-ranges.terroir: Granite-derived sandy soils; about 1,620 growing degree days.

au-sunbury.name: Sunbury
au-sunbury.summary: A small region just north-west of Melbourne airport, with a nineteenth-century heritage: Craiglee's bluestone winery was built in 1864, and its 1872 Hermitage was still being opened in the twentieth century. Today Craiglee and Galli Estate make peppery Shiraz and Chardonnay.
au-sunbury.terroir: Dry (about 530 mm), windy plains with volcanic soils.
au-sunbury.nerd_note: Goona Warra, also at Sunbury, has a bluestone winery from 1863.

au-swan-district.name: Swan District
au-swan-district.summary: The region north and east of Perth along the Swan River, containing the Swan Valley subregion, one of the hottest fine-wine regions in Australia. Its hot, dry summers once made it the centre of Western Australian fortified wine.
au-swan-district.terroir: About 2,570 growing degree days; under 150 mm of rain from October to April.

au-swan-hill.name: Swan Hill
au-swan-hill.summary: An irrigated Murray River region around Swan Hill and Robinvale, straddling Victoria and New South Wales, producing about 35,000 to 47,000 tonnes a year for branded and bulk wine. Like the Murray Darling region downstream, it depends entirely on river water allocations, which in drought years can decide the size of the crop.
au-swan-hill.terroir: Hot (about 2,360 growing degree days), very dry (329 mm), irrigated.

au-swan-valley.name: Swan Valley
au-swan-valley.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Verdelho, Grenache, Shiraz, Muscat, Pedro Ximénez
au-swan-valley.summary: Western Australia's oldest wine district, 25 minutes from Perth's centre, registered as a subregion in 2003. Thomas Waters planted Olive Farm in 1830, and Houghton (1836) became famous for its 'White Burgundy', a Chenin-based blend created by Jack Mann in 1937 that was Australia's best-selling white for decades. Croatian families such as the Kosoviches (Westfield) and Yurisiches settled here in the early twentieth century. Today it makes dry Chenin and Verdelho, fortified 'liqueur' wines and generous reds.
au-swan-valley.terroir: Hot (about 2,570 growing degree days) and dry, with deep alluvial loams and sands along the river.
au-swan-valley.nerd_note: Houghton's White Burgundy was renamed White Classic after the EU wine agreement retired 'Burgundy' on Australian labels.

au-tasmania.name: Tasmania
au-tasmania.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Riesling
au-tasmania.summary:
Tasmania is one GI that works as a state, zone and region at once, and it has become the most dynamic fine-wine area in Australia. With fewer than 800 growing degree days on Wine Australia's figures, it is the only part of the country with a climate truly comparable to Champagne or Burgundy, and its 1,700 ha now supply most of Australia's best traditional-method sparkling and a growing share of its best Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Large mainland companies (Accolade, Treasury, Brown Brothers) bought Tasmanian vineyards and wineries from the 1990s to secure cool-climate fruit.

The island's informal areas differ sharply. The north, the Tamar Valley and Pipers River, is cooler and wetter; Pipers River, close to Bass Strait, gives the tightest sparkling base (Jansz, Pipers Brook). The south-east, in the rain shadow of the central highlands, is drier and sunnier: the Coal River Valley around Richmond and Cambridge (Tolpuddle, Domaine A, Frogmore Creek, Pooley) and the Derwent Valley (Stefano Lubiana, Moorilla, Derwent Estate) make riper Pinot and Chardonnay. The East Coast around Swansea and Freycinet is warm by Tasmanian standards, and the Huon Valley and D'Entrecasteaux Channel in the far south are the coolest of all.

Ed Carr's House of Arras, with sparkling wines aged up to a decade or more on lees, and Jansz, the Yalumba-owned house founded with Louis Roederer in 1985, are the sparkling references; Tolpuddle, bought in 2011 by Martin Shaw and Michael Hill Smith of Shaw + Smith, Stefano Lubiana (biodynamic), Dawson James and Sailor Seeks Horse lead for Pinot and Chardonnay.
au-tasmania.terroir: Cool and maritime, with long, slow autumns. Wine Australia records about 790 growing degree days and 585 mm of growing-season rain (the north is wetter, the south-east drier). Soils include red basalt-derived krasnozems at Pipers River, dolerite and sandstone in the south, and alluvial gravels along the Tamar and Derwent.
au-tasmania.nerd_note: Tasmania's oldest wine estate in operation, Providence near Launceston, began in 1956 as La Provence; its French name was changed after a challenge from the French appellation authorities.

au-the-peninsulas.name: The Peninsulas
au-the-peninsulas.summary: A zone covering the Eyre and Yorke peninsulas west of Adelaide, with about 70 ha of scattered vineyards, notably around Boston Bay near Port Lincoln and on Yorke Peninsula. It has no registered regions.

au-tumbarumba.name: Tumbarumba
au-tumbarumba.summary: High in the western foothills of the Snowy Mountains at 300 to 800 m, Tumbarumba grows some of Australia's finest Chardonnay and sparkling base for big companies. It was badly hit by the 2019 to 2020 bushfires.
au-tumbarumba.terroir: About 1,720 growing degree days; granite and basalt soils; cold nights and frost risk.
au-tumbarumba.nerd_note: Penfolds' Yattarna Chardonnay has included Tumbarumba fruit.

au-upper-goulburn.name: Upper Goulburn
au-upper-goulburn.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc
au-upper-goulburn.summary: Hilly country around Mansfield, Alexandra and Lake Eildon at the foot of the Victorian Alps, registered in 2003. Delatite, founded by the Ritchie family in 1968, is its best-known estate, with aromatic whites and biodynamic farming.
au-upper-goulburn.terroir: Elevations up to about 1,000 m, cool (about 1,540 growing degree days).

au-upper-hunter-valley.name: Upper Hunter Valley
au-upper-hunter-valley.summary: The upper reaches of the Hunter around Denman and Muswellbrook, registered in 2010. Rosemount Estate, founded at Denman in 1969, made its Roxburgh Chardonnay here; the area is drier and warmer than the Lower Hunter.
au-upper-hunter-valley.terroir: Black and red clay and limestone soils; irrigated in many places.

au-victoria.name: Victoria
au-victoria.grapes: Shiraz, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscat
au-victoria.summary: The state GI for Victoria, used for blends across its 21 regions. Victoria has more registered regions than any other state, reflecting a climate range from the hot Murray to the cold Macedon Ranges, and the family-scale, region-driven industry that rebuilt itself after phylloxera.
au-victoria.terroir: Cool maritime south, alpine centre and north-east, hot irrigated north-west.
au-victoria.nerd_note: In the 1880s Victoria produced more wine than New South Wales and South Australia combined; phylloxera and the 1890s depression ended that.

au-west-australian-south-east-coastal.name: West Australian South East Coastal
au-west-australian-south-east-coastal.summary: A coastal zone around Esperance with almost no vineyards. It exists, like several outback zones, so that every part of Western Australia is covered by a GI.

au-western-australia.name: Western Australia
au-western-australia.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Shiraz, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon
au-western-australia.summary: The state GI for Western Australia. The state is outside the South Eastern Australia super zone, so its blends cannot carry that name; Western Australian wineries use this GI or their region.
contains: Eastern Plains, Inland and North of Western Australia

au-western-plains.name: Western Plains
au-western-plains.summary: A vast zone covering western New South Wales, with almost no vineyards and no regions. The zone exists so that every part of the state is covered by a GI.

au-western-victoria.name: Western Victoria
au-western-victoria.summary: The zone of western Victoria's ranges and plains: Grampians (with Great Western), Pyrenees and Henty. It is one of the coolest parts of the state, and its historic centre is the gold-rush town of Great Western, where wine has been made at Best's and at the cellars that became Seppelt since the 1860s.

au-wrattonbully.name: Wrattonbully
au-wrattonbully.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Tempranillo
au-wrattonbully.summary: Wrattonbully sits just north of Coonawarra and shares its terra rossa over limestone, but its land is more undulating and less prone to frost, and it ripens grapes a little earlier. Most vineyards date from the 1990s, many owned by big companies whose fruit goes into Coonawarra-style blends. Brian Croser's Tapanappa makes its Whalebone Vineyard Cabernet Shiraz here from vines planted in 1974, named for a 35-million-year-old whale skeleton found in a cave beneath it.
au-wrattonbully.terroir: About 1,650 growing degree days; terra rossa and sandy loam over limestone, at 75 to 150 m, with caves and sinkholes in the karst below.
au-wrattonbully.nerd_note: The Naracoorte Caves, a World Heritage fossil site, lie at the region's edge in the same limestone.

au-yarra-valley.name: Yarra Valley
au-yarra-valley.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Sauvignon Blanc, Nebbiolo
au-yarra-valley.summary:
The Yarra Valley, an hour east of Melbourne, was Victoria's first wine region and is its most celebrated. Swiss settlers planted it from the 1840s: Paul de Castella at Yering Station, his brother Hubert at St Hubert's and Guillaume de Pury at Yeringberg. In 1889 a Yering wine won a grand prix at the Paris Exposition. Then fashion, phylloxera fears and the dairy industry wiped it out; the last vintage at Yeringberg in its first life was 1921.

Doctors and scientists brought it back. Dr Reg Egan replanted Wantirna Estate in 1963, Dr Bailey Carrodus founded Yarra Yering in 1969 and Dr John Middleton Mount Mary in 1971, both making Bordeaux and Burgundy styles of rare finesse. Moët & Chandon chose the valley for Domaine Chandon in 1986, and since the 2000s producers such as Giant Steps, Oakridge, Mac Forbes, Yarra Yering under Sarah Crowe, and Timo Mayer have made it Australia's best-known source of elegant Pinot Noir and tight, struck-match Chardonnay, as well as perfumed, medium-bodied Shiraz and Cabernet.

The region is split by geology and altitude. The lower, warmer valley floor and northern slopes (Coldstream, Dixons Creek, Gruyere) suit Cabernet and Shiraz on grey sandy clay loams; the Upper Yarra (Hoddles Creek, Seville, Woori Yallock), on deep red volcanic soils at up to about 400 m, is cooler and wetter and makes taut Chardonnay and Pinot. Wine Australia records about 1,440 growing degree days, among the coolest of mainland Australia's major regions.
au-yarra-valley.terroir: Rainfall around 1,080 mm a year and 550 mm in the growing season, high for Australia. Grey sandy loams over clay and sandstone on the valley floor and northern hillsides; red volcanic krasnozem in the Upper Yarra. Bushfires (2009) and smoke taint (2020) are recurring risks.
au-yarra-valley.nerd_note: Mount Mary's Quintet is a blend of all five Bordeaux reds, and until 2008 the estate sold almost entirely by mailing list; Dr Middleton refused to enter wine shows.

sites.name: Langmeil Freedom 1843 Vineyard
sites.text: Langmeil's winery on the North Para River at Tanunda stands beside the Freedom vineyard, a block of Shiraz planted in 1843 by Christian Auricht, a Silesian settler. It is generally cited as the oldest continuously producing Shiraz vineyard in the world. The Lindner family bought the site in 1996, and the wine, Freedom 1843 Shiraz, comes from about 3.5 acres of gnarled, own-rooted vines.

sites.name: Turkey Flat
sites.text: The Schulz family's Turkey Flat at Bethany, on the southern edge of Tanunda, holds Shiraz planted in 1847 by Johann Fiedler, a Silesian settler, among the oldest vines in the Barossa. The cellar door is in the old butcher's shop and bluestone cottage. Turkey Flat also helped revive Barossa Grenache and Mataro rosé.

sites.name: Seppeltsfield
sites.text: Joseph Seppelt, a Silesian snuff and tobacco merchant, bought land here in 1851 and built a wine village of bluestone cellars. In 1878 his son Benno laid down a barrel of Tawny to be opened in 1978, beginning the Centennial Collection, the world's only unbroken run of single-vintage Tawny since 1878. Each year the 100-year-old Para Vintage Tawny is released (the 1926 in 2026), in 100 ml bottles.
sites.class: Centennial Collection, 100 Year Old Para Vintage Tawny

sites.name: Seppelt Family Mausoleum
sites.text: A Doric-columned mausoleum built in 1927 on a hill above Seppeltsfield, reached along an avenue of about 2,000 date palms planted by Seppelt workers during the Depression of the 1930s. It is one of the most photographed landmarks in Australian wine.

sites.name: Yalumba
sites.text: Founded in 1849 at Angaston by Samuel Smith, an English brewer, Yalumba is Australia's oldest family-owned winery, now run by the fifth generation of the Hill-Smith family. Its blue-marble clock-tower winery dates from 1908, and it is one of the few Australian wineries with its own cooperage. Yalumba drafted the Barossa Old Vine Charter in 2007 and planted Viognier in the Eden Valley in 1980, a pioneering move.

sites.name: Chateau Tanunda
sites.text: Built in 1890 from Bethany bluestone in eleven months, Chateau Tanunda was said to be the largest building in the Southern Hemisphere when finished, a co-operative winery and distillery designed to exploit Europe's phylloxera shortage. Seppelt owned it from 1916 to 1998; the Geber family restored it and its cellars, and it is on the South Australian Heritage Register.

sites.name: Rockford
sites.text: Robert O'Callaghan's Rockford, founded in 1984 in old stone buildings at Krondorf, became the conscience of the Barossa during the 1980s vine-pull years by buying old-vine fruit from growers and making it with 1880s machinery, including a hand-fed basket press. Its Basket Press Shiraz and cellar-door-only Black Shiraz (a sparkling red) are cult wines.

sites.name: Torbreck
sites.text: Founded by David Powell in 1994 at Marananga, in the northern-central Barossa, Torbreck built its reputation on old-vine Shiraz, Grenache and Mataro sourced from family growers, and on Rhône-inspired blends such as RunRig (Shiraz with a little Viognier). It became one of the defining names of the 1990s and 2000s Barossa boom.

sites.name: Penfolds Kalimna (Block 42)
sites.text: Penfolds bought the Kalimna vineyard near Moppa in the northern Barossa in 1945. Its Block 42, planted around 1888, is thought to be the oldest continuously producing Cabernet Sauvignon vineyard in the world, and is bottled separately only in rare years. Kalimna fruit has been a backbone of Grange.

sites.name: Cirillo Old Vines, Light Pass
sites.text: The Cirillo family's Grenache at Light Pass was planted in 1848 on deep sand and still grows on its own roots; it is among the oldest Grenache vines in the world. The family bought the vineyard in 1969, and the wine is named The Vincent after Vincenzo Cirillo.

sites.name: Hewitson Old Garden, Rowland Flat
sites.text: A block of Mourvèdre at Rowland Flat planted in 1853, said to be the oldest Mourvèdre vines in the world. Dean Hewitson bought it in 1998 and has propagated cuttings from it, partly to safeguard the genetic material.

sites.name: Jacob's Creek Visitor Centre
sites.text: Johann Gramp planted the first commercial vineyard in the Barossa beside Jacob's Creek at Rowland Flat in 1847. His company, Orlando, made the first Jacob's Creek red from the 1973 vintage and turned it into one of the best-known Australian wines abroad.

sites.name: Peter Lehmann Wines
sites.text: When an oversupply in the late 1970s left Barossa growers with no buyer, Peter Lehmann, then winemaker at Saltram, kept buying their grapes and founded his own company in 1979. His guarantee helped save many old vineyards from the government-funded vine pull of the 1980s.

sites.name: Henschke, Keyneton
sites.text: Johann Christian Henschke, a Silesian stonemason, began making wine at Keyneton in 1868, and the family's sixth generation now runs it. Cyril Henschke released Hill of Grace as a single-vineyard wine with the 1958 vintage, and Stephen and Prue Henschke turned the estate into a leader of sustainable and biodynamic viticulture.

sites.name: Hill of Grace
sites.text: An eight-hectare vineyard opposite the Gnadenberg (Hill of Grace) Lutheran church near Moculta, planted by Nicolaus Stanitzki in the 1860s. Its oldest Shiraz vines, the 'Grandfathers', are around 160 years old and still own-rooted. Hill of Grace Shiraz is Australia's most famous single-vineyard wine after Grange.

sites.name: Mount Edelstone
sites.text: A 16-hectare Shiraz vineyard near Keyneton, planted in 1912 by Ronald Angas and bought by Cyril Henschke in 1974. Its wine, first made as a single vineyard in 1952, is one of Australia's longest-running single-vineyard Shiraz labels.

sites.name: Pewsey Vale
sites.text: Joseph Gilbert planted Pewsey Vale in the High Eden hills in 1847. Yalumba replanted it in 1961 after decades of grazing, and its terraced Riesling vineyard, at nearly 500 m, now produces The Contours, a Riesling released with five years in bottle.

sites.name: Grosset, Auburn
sites.text: Jeffrey Grosset opened his winery in a former dairy factory in Auburn in 1981. He led the 2000 Clare Valley screwcap initiative and makes two benchmark Rieslings that show the region's split: Polish Hill (slate, austere) and Springvale (red loam over limestone at Watervale).

sites.name: Polish Hill River
sites.text: A side valley east of Sevenhill settled by Polish immigrants from 1856, whose stone church of St Stanislaus Kostka (1871) is now a museum. The valley's hard slate and shale soils produce the leanest, most mineral Clare Rieslings, including Grosset's Polish Hill, first made in 1981.

sites.name: Sevenhill Cellars
sites.text: Austrian Jesuits fleeing persecution founded Sevenhill in 1851 and planted vines to make sacramental wine. It is the oldest winery in the Clare Valley and still run by the Jesuits, with St Aloysius' church (1875) and a crypt beneath it on the property.

sites.name: Wendouree
sites.text: A winery founded in 1895 near Clare whose old, dry-grown Shiraz, Malbec, Cabernet and Mataro are made by Tony Brady and family in the same slate-walled cellar. Wendouree sells almost entirely by mailing list, has no cellar door or website, and its tannic reds need two decades.

sites.name: Jim Barry Wines
sites.text: Jim Barry, the first qualified winemaker to work in the Clare Valley (1947), founded this company in 1959. The Armagh Shiraz, first made in 1985, is its flagship, and in 2016 it released Australia's first commercial Assyrtiko, from cuttings imported from Santorini.

sites.name: Kilikanoon
sites.text: A Clare producer founded at Penwortham in 1997, whose old-vine Shiraz (Oracle, Attunga 1865 from vines planted in 1865) and Mort's Block Riesling from Watervale are regional benchmarks. Its cellar door sits in a stone building among the vines in the centre of the valley.

sites.name: d'Arenberg Cube
sites.text: A five-storey glass building opened in 2017 at d'Arenberg, McLaren Vale, inspired by a Rubik's cube and designed to look as if it is floating above the vines. d'Arenberg was founded by Joseph Osborn in 1912 and is run by Chester Osborn, who still foot-treads and basket-presses reds. The Dead Arm Shiraz is named after a vine disease (Eutypa) that kills one arm of the vine.

sites.name: Clarendon Hills Astralis
sites.text: Roman Bratasiuk's Clarendon Hills sources from old, dry-grown vines in the hills above Clarendon, at the northern edge of McLaren Vale. Astralis Shiraz, first made in 1994 from vines planted in the 1920s, became one of Australia's most expensive wines; the estate also bottles single-vineyard Grenache such as Romas and Blewitt Springs.

sites.name: Hardys Tintara
sites.text: Thomas Hardy, who arrived in South Australia in 1850, bought the Tintara winery in McLaren Vale in 1876 and built the company that became Australia's largest. The old Tintara cellars on the main road still house a cellar door; the Hardy family's vineyards include Sauvignon Blanc planted in the 1870s.

sites.name: Chateau Reynella
sites.text: John Reynell planted vines here in 1838, two years after South Australia was founded, and dug an underground cellar in 1845, one of the first winery buildings in the state. The property, now the headquarters of the Hardys business, holds the Old Cave Cellar.

sites.name: Wirra Wirra
sites.text: Founded in 1894 by Robert Strangways Wigley, a cricket-loving eccentric, and revived in 1969 by Greg and Roger Trott. Its ironstone-walled winery and flagship RSW Shiraz and Church Block blend are McLaren Vale fixtures.

sites.name: Coriole
sites.text: The Lloyd family's Coriole, around an 1860 stone farmhouse, planted Sangiovese in 1985 and Fiano in 2000, early moves that helped make McLaren Vale Australia's laboratory for Mediterranean varieties.

sites.name: Bleasdale
sites.text: Frank Potts founded Bleasdale at Langhorne Creek in 1850 and the family still runs it. Its red gum lever press, built in 1892 from a single tree, worked until 1960; Potts also flooded the vineyards in winter by diverting the Bremer River.

sites.name: Shaw + Smith
sites.text: Founded in 1989 by Michael Hill Smith, Australia's first Master of Wine, and his cousin Martin Shaw. Their Adelaide Hills Sauvignon Blanc became a national benchmark; their M3 Chardonnay and Shiraz followed, and in 2011 they bought Tolpuddle in Tasmania.

sites.name: Penfolds Magill Estate
sites.text: Dr Christopher Rawson Penfold and his wife Mary planted vines at their cottage, The Grange, in 1844. Max Schubert made the first experimental Grange Hermitage here in 1951. Penfolds still makes the Magill Estate Shiraz from the five-hectare suburban vineyard, one of the few urban single-vineyard wines in the world, and the restored Grange cottage is on site.

sites.name: Wynns Coonawarra Estate
sites.text: John Riddoch built this triple-gabled limestone winery in 1891 for his Penola Fruit Colony. The Wynn family bought it in 1951; its gabled facade, drawn by artist Richard Beck, became the emblem of Coonawarra on every Wynns label. It makes the Black Label Cabernet (from 1954) and the John Riddoch Cabernet (from 1982).

sites.name: Yallum Park
sites.text: John Riddoch's homestead near Penola, built in 1880 for the pastoralist who founded the Coonawarra fruit colony in 1890. The Riddochs held huge pastoral runs across the south-east; Yallum Park is now a private heritage house.

sites.name: Majella
sites.text: The Lynn family were Coonawarra sheep farmers who planted vines in 1968 and sold grapes to Wynns before making their own wine from 1991. Majella's The Malleea Cabernet Shiraz is a classic Coonawarra blend.

sites.name: Tahbilk
sites.text: Founded in 1860 on the Goulburn River and owned by the Purbrick family since 1925, Tahbilk is the oldest family-owned winery in Victoria. A small block of Shiraz planted in 1860 survived phylloxera on its sandy soils and makes the 1860 Vines Shiraz; the estate also has one of the world's oldest and largest plantings of Marsanne (from 1927). Its 1860 cellars and tower are classified by the National Trust.

sites.name: Mitchelton
sites.text: Founded in 1969 on the Goulburn River near Nagambie, with a 55-metre observation tower that is a local landmark; Mitchelton helped revive Marsanne and Rhône varieties in Victoria.

sites.name: Best's Great Western, Concongella
sites.text: Henry Best planted Concongella in 1866, and the Thomson family has owned it since 1920. Its Nursery Block, planted in the 1860s, holds about 40 varieties, some still unidentified, and the world's oldest Pinot Meunier and Dolcetto vines; the 1868 slab-and-timber cellars are still in use.

sites.name: Seppelt Great Western drives
sites.text: Miners dug about 3 km of tunnels, called 'drives', into the hillside at Great Western from 1868 for Hans Irvine, who made traditional-method sparkling wine here. Seppelt bought the business in 1918 and used the drives to age 'Great Western' sparkling and the famous sparkling Shiraz. The drives are National Trust classified.

sites.name: Chambers Rosewood
sites.text: The Chambers family has made fortified wine at Rutherglen since 1858. Its Rare Muscat and Rare Muscadelle are blended from soleras that include wine laid down in the 1890s, and are among the most acclaimed fortified wines in the world. The cellar door is a working shed.

sites.name: Morris
sites.text: The Morris family has made wine near Rutherglen since George Francis Morris planted in 1859; by the 1880s his Fairfield winery was said to be one of the largest in the Southern Hemisphere. Mick and David Morris built its reputation for Muscat and Topaque; Old Premium Rare Muscat is the flagship.

sites.name: Campbells
sites.text: John Campbell, a Scottish gold miner, planted vines at Bobbie Burns in 1870, and the family still owns the winery. Campbells makes Muscat and Topaque on the four-tier Rutherglen ladder, with Merchant Prince Rare Muscat at the top, and Bobbie Burns Shiraz.

sites.name: All Saints Estate
sites.text: A turreted red-brick castle at Wahgunyah built in 1880s style by George Sutherland Smith, a Scottish carpenter, modelled on the Castle of Mey. The estate has made fortified wine since 1864 and is now owned by the Brown family (Eileen Brown and her children).

sites.name: Brown Brothers, Milawa
sites.text: John Francis Brown made his first wine at Milawa in 1889, and the family still runs one of Australia's largest family wineries. Brown Brothers pioneered variety trials in its Kindergarten winery and helped popularise Moscato and Prosecco in Australia.

sites.name: Giaconda
sites.text: Rick Kinzbrunner planted Giaconda on a steep granite slope at Everton Upper in 1982. Its Chardonnay, wild-fermented and aged in a cellar blasted into the granite, is one of Australia's most sought-after whites; production is tiny.

sites.name: Bass Phillip
sites.text: Phillip Jones planted close-spaced, unirrigated Pinot Noir at Leongatha South in 1979 on deep red soil and made wines compared with Burgundy. Burgundian Jean-Marie Fourrier and partners bought the estate in 2020.

sites.name: Mount Mary
sites.text: Dr John Middleton, a Melbourne physician, planted Mount Mary at Lilydale in 1971. Its Quintet (all five Bordeaux red varieties) and Triolet (Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Muscadelle) are among Australia's most elegant wines, sold mostly by mailing list.

sites.name: Yarra Yering
sites.text: Dr Bailey Carrodus, a plant physiologist, planted Yarra Yering on a north-facing slope at Gruyere in 1969. His Dry Red No. 1 (Cabernet blend) and Dry Red No. 2 (Shiraz blend) were unlike anything else in Australia; Sarah Crowe has made the wines since 2013.

sites.name: Yeringberg
sites.text: Guillaume de Pury, a Swiss from Neuchâtel, founded Yeringberg in 1863, and his descendants still own it. Wine stopped in 1921 and resumed in 1969 in the original 1885 three-storey gravity winery.

sites.name: Domaine Chandon Australia
sites.text: Moët & Chandon's Australian outpost, founded at Coldstream in 1986 on the old Green Point farm, helped prove that the Yarra Valley could make serious traditional-method sparkling wine.

sites.name: De Bortoli Yarra Valley
sites.text: The Riverina's De Bortoli family bought a Dixons Creek vineyard in 1987, and Steve Webber and Leanne De Bortoli turned it into a leader of lighter, more transparent Yarra Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

sites.name: Paringa Estate
sites.text: Lindsay McCall, a schoolteacher, planted Paringa at Red Hill South in 1985; its Pinot Noir and Shiraz won national trophies and put the Mornington Peninsula on the map.

sites.name: Ten Minutes by Tractor
sites.text: Named after the time it takes to drive a tractor between its original three vineyards, this Mornington Peninsula producer makes single-vineyard Pinot and Chardonnay that show the peninsula's site differences.

sites.name: Bannockburn Vineyards
sites.text: Stuart Hooper planted Bannockburn in the Moorabool Valley in 1974; Gary Farr, its winemaker for 20 years, worked vintages at Domaine Dujac. The close-planted Serré Pinot Noir is its icon.

sites.name: Jasper Hill
sites.text: Ron and Elva Laughton planted Jasper Hill on Heathcote's Cambrian greenstone in 1975, dry-grown and own-rooted. Georgia's Paddock and Emily's Paddock Shiraz made the region's reputation.

sites.name: Balgownie Estate, Bendigo
sites.text: Stuart Anderson, a pharmacist, planted Balgownie at Maiden Gully in 1969, reviving viticulture in Bendigo after phylloxera and government-ordered uprooting had ended it about 70 years earlier. Its Shiraz and Cabernet, firm and minty, made Bendigo a fine-wine name again.

sites.name: Dalwhinnie
sites.text: A Pyrenees estate at Moonambel planted in 1976 in an amphitheatre of hills, known for structured, long-lived Shiraz and Cabernet from dry-grown vines on quartz gravel at around 500 to 600 m. It is one of the region's most consistent producers.

sites.name: Farm Cove
sites.text: The first vines in Australia were planted at Farm Cove on Sydney Harbour in 1788, from cuttings the First Fleet collected at Rio de Janeiro and the Cape. They failed in the humid climate; the site is now part of the Royal Botanic Garden.

sites.name: Elizabeth Farm
sites.text: John and Elizabeth Macarthur's farmhouse at Parramatta (1793), the oldest surviving European building in Australia. The Macarthurs' sons later planted vines at Camden Park and sent wine to London; Elizabeth Farm is now a museum.

sites.name: Dalwood Estate
sites.text: George Wyndham bought Dalwood on the Hunter River in 1828 and planted vines there in 1830, among the first in the valley. Penfolds later owned it; it is now a small estate again.

sites.name: Tyrrell's
sites.text: Edward Tyrrell planted at Ashmans in 1858, and the family's fifth generation runs it. Vat 1 Semillon is the archetypal Hunter Semillon; Vat 47 (1971) was Australia's first commercial varietal Chardonnay, and the Old Patch Shiraz vines date from 1867.

sites.name: Mount Pleasant
sites.text: Maurice O'Shea, trained in France, made wine at Mount Pleasant from 1921 until his death in 1956, and his medium-bodied 'Hunter Burgundy' reds and Semillons are legendary. McWilliam's took full control in 1941, and the estate passed to new private owners in 2021 when McWilliam's was sold up; vines planted in 1880 and 1921 still crop.

sites.name: Lake's Folly
sites.text: Dr Max Lake, a Sydney surgeon, planted Cabernet Sauvignon at Pokolbin in 1963, the first new vineyard in the Hunter for decades and the start of Australia's boutique winery movement.

sites.name: Clonakilla
sites.text: CSIRO scientist John Kirk planted Clonakilla at Murrumbateman in 1971. His son Tim, inspired by Côte-Rôtie, co-fermented Shiraz with a little Viognier from 1992, creating one of Australia's most influential wines.

sites.name: Helm Wines
sites.text: Ken Helm, descended from German vignerons, founded Helm at Murrumbateman in 1973 in a nineteenth-century schoolhouse. He champions dry Riesling, founded the Canberra International Riesling Challenge in 2000, and helped make the Canberra District one of Australia's Riesling regions.

sites.name: Philip Shaw
sites.text: Former Rosemount chief winemaker Philip Shaw planted the Koomooloo vineyard on the slopes of Mount Canobolas in 1989, at about 900 m on volcanic soils. His Chardonnay and Shiraz helped build Orange's cool-climate reputation, and his sons now run the estate.

sites.name: Vasse Felix
sites.text: Dr Tom Cullity, a Perth cardiologist, planted Margaret River's first commercial vineyard here in 1967 after reading John Gladstones' climate research. Vasse Felix is now known for its Heytesbury Chardonnay and Tom Cullity Cabernet.

sites.name: Moss Wood
sites.text: Dr Bill Pannell planted Moss Wood at Wilyabrup in 1969; Keith and Clare Mugford have owned it since 1985. Its Cabernet Sauvignon is one of Australia's most consistent and long-lived.

sites.name: Cullen Wines
sites.text: Kevin and Diana Cullen planted at Wilyabrup in 1971; their daughter Vanya made the estate biodynamic and carbon-neutral. The Diana Madeline Cabernet blend is a Margaret River benchmark.

sites.name: Leeuwin Estate
sites.text: Denis and Tricia Horgan founded Leeuwin in 1974 with advice from Robert Mondavi. Its Art Series Chardonnay, first made in 1980, is often called Australia's finest white wine; the estate's concerts on the lawn have run since 1985.

sites.name: Voyager Estate
sites.text: A white Cape Dutch-style estate on Stevens Road, planted in 1978 and bought by mining magnate Michael Wright in 1991. Voyager is known for Chardonnay and Cabernet from the cooler southern part of Margaret River, and now farms organically.

sites.name: Houghton
sites.text: Founded in 1836 in the Swan Valley and named after Colonel Richard Houghton, one of the original partners. Jack Mann, winemaker from 1930 to 1972, created Houghton White Burgundy (1937), Australia's best-selling white for decades.

sites.name: Sandalford
sites.text: John Septimus Roe, Western Australia's first Surveyor-General, was granted land on the Swan River in 1840; the family began making wine commercially here, and the estate's jetty still serves wine-cruise boats from Perth.

sites.name: Frankland Estate
sites.text: Barrie Smith and Judi Cullam planted vines on their sheep farm at Frankland River in 1988; their Isolation Ridge Riesling and organic farming helped make the Great Southern a Riesling region.

sites.name: Plantagenet
sites.text: Tony Smith, an English-born farmer, planted Plantagenet near Mount Barker in 1968, the first commercial winery in the Great Southern, in a former apple-packing shed.

sites.name: Castle Rock Estate
sites.text: Angelo and Wendy Diletti's vineyards on the north-facing granite slopes of the Porongurup Range were planted in 1981, above the frost line. Their delicate, mineral, long-lived Rieslings and fine Pinot Noir define the subregion's style.

sites.name: Stefano Lubiana
sites.text: Steve and Monique Lubiana moved from South Australia's Riverland to the Derwent Valley in 1990 and built a biodynamic estate making Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and long-aged sparkling.

sites.name: Tolpuddle Vineyard
sites.text: Planted in 1988 in the Coal River Valley near Richmond and named after the Tolpuddle Martyrs, one of whom was transported to Tasmania. Shaw + Smith bought it in 2011, and its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are among Australia's best.

sites.name: Josef Chromy
sites.text: Josef Chromy fled Czechoslovakia in 1950, became a butcher in Launceston, and later invested in Tasmanian wine (Rochecombe, Jansz). His own estate at Relbia, in the Tamar Valley, opened in 2007.

sites.name: Jansz
sites.text: Founded in 1985 at Pipers River as a joint venture with Champagne Louis Roederer and now owned by Yalumba's Hill-Smith family, Jansz showed that Tasmania could make serious traditional-method sparkling wine.

sites.name: Ballandean Estate
sites.text: The Puglisi family's estate in the Granite Belt traces its vines to 1932, when Italian migrants grew grapes on the granite plateau near Stanthorpe; it is Queensland's oldest family-owned winery.
